27.5.6     Positive-feature Sinkhorn
A related route factorizes the kernel through positive features rather than through land-
mark columns [Scetbon and Cuturi, 2020]. Choose a nonnegative feature map

                                           ϕθ (x) ∈ Rr+                           (27.27)

and define the induced kernel

                                Kθ (xi , xj ) = ⟨ϕθ (xi ), ϕθ (xj )⟩.             (27.28)

The corresponding cost representation is then

                                cθ (xi , xj ) = −ε log Kθ (xi , xj ).             (27.29)

At the matrix level, define source and target feature collections by

                                  Ξ = [ϕθ (x1 ), . . . , ϕθ (xN )],               (27.30)
                                  Z = [ϕθ (z1 ), . . . , ϕθ (zN )],               (27.31)

so the sample kernel factorizes as
                                           Kθ = Ξ′ Z.                             (27.32)
Balancing steps can therefore be expressed through feature-space products rather than
through a materialized dense kernel. After the feature matrices are formed, the dominant
kernel-vector products scale like O(r(N + N )), so the attraction is again execution-path
efficiency rather than a new transport doctrine.
    The same factorization also has a useful integral reading. One may view the kernel
as arising from a positive feature integral
                                       Z
                             k(x, y) =    ϕ(x, u)′ ϕ(y, u) dρ(u),                  (27.33)
                                           U

and then approximate that integral by a finite feature family,
                                    1
                           ϕθ (x) = √ (ϕ(x, u1 ), . . . , ϕ(x, ur )).             (27.34)
                                     r

This explains why the factorized kernel should still be read as an approximation to the
teacher-side kernel action, not automatically as the exact original kernel. The corre-
sponding factored transport application is

                                P X = diag(u)Ξ′ Z diag(v)X.                       (27.35)

This gives the same pedagogical ladder as Nystr”om:

  (i) replace dense kernel application by a factorized kernel action,

 (ii) run the retained balancing logic through the factors,

(iii) judge the corrected route by teacher-preservation residuals rather than by runtime
      alone.
262           CHAPTER 27. RETAINED-TEACHER NEURAL OT WARM STARTS

One can also write the induced entropic dual in factorized form,

                    Wε,cθ (µ, ν) = max a′ α + b′ β − ε(Ξeα/ε )′ Zeβ/ε + ε,          (27.36)
                                    α,β


which makes the same point from the dual side: the expensive dense interaction is replaced
by feature-space products. The caution is sharper than for a pure engineering variant. A
positive-feature route changes the effective kernel representation and therefore must be
judged by teacher-preservation residuals, marginal checks, and transported-cloud parity,
not by runtime alone. It is retained-teacher only to the extent that the corrected route
is still explicitly audited against the chosen teacher object.


27.5.7     Direct low-rank coupling approximations
Kernel approximations are not the only retained-family option. One may also factorize
the coupling itself [Forrow et al., 2019, Scetbon et al., 2021, Scetbon and Cuturi, 2022,
Scetbon et al., 2023]. The key conceptual distinction is:

      Approximating the kernel asks how to preserve the same teacher-side trans-
      port from a compressed kernel action. Constraining the coupling asks whether
      a restricted family of couplings is already sufficient.

The second route is more than a fast matvec; it changes the feasible family being searched.
  A useful formal entry point is the nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix,
                          (            r
                                                                        )
                                      X
        rank+ (M ) = min r : M =         Mk , rank(Mk ) = 1, Mk ≥ 0 .               (27.37)
                                           k=1

The rank-constrained coupling family is then

                          Πa,b (r) = {P ∈ Π(a, b) : rank+ (P ) ≤ r}.                (27.38)

A generic factorized parameterization is

                                    P = Q diag(1/g)R′ ,                             (27.39)

with factor constraints

                          Q ∈ Π(a, g),         R ∈ Π(b, g),   g ∈ ∆r .              (27.40)

These constraints mean that the factors themselves carry source mass a, target mass b,
and an intermediate latent mass profile g. Equivalently, one may speak of the factored
feasible family

               F Ca,b (r) = {(Q, R, g) : Q ∈ Π(a, g), R ∈ Π(b, g), g ∈ ∆r },        (27.41)

so the low-rank optimization problem can be read either as a search over rank-constrained
couplings or as a search over factored feasible triples. In the same notation, the objective
itself is
                      min ⟨C, P ⟩ =       min        ⟨C, Q diag(1/g)R′ ⟩ .           (27.42)
                   P ∈Πa,b (r)           (Q,R,g)∈F Ca,b (r)
27.5. EVIDENCE CONTRACT FOR RETAINED-TEACHER LEARNING                                   263

Transport application then becomes

                                 P X = Q diag(1/g)R′ X,                             (27.43)

so storage and barycentric application are both executed through the low-rank factors
rather than through a dense coupling.
   A richer extension introduces a small latent transport plan T between the two factor
families. In schematic form, the induced coupling becomes

                            P = Q diag(1/gQ )T diag(1/gR )R′ ,                      (27.44)

which allows mass to route through a compact latent transport instead of only through
diagonal latent components. A practical rank-adequacy question then appears: is the
chosen rank large enough? The note’s stronger low-rank lines use reduced-gradient or
dual-slack diagnostics for that purpose. Even without carrying those full certificates into
this chapter, the reader should keep the right lesson in view: low-rank coupling is not only
a storage trick; it is an optimization over a restricted feasible family, so parity against
the teacher must be checked whenever rank is fixed in advance.
    For the present chapter, the important boundary is interpretive. If the first test
remains teacher-preservation parity after correction, then the family can still be read
through the retained-teacher lens. If the prose instead starts defending the restricted
family as a different final transport object in its own right, the discussion has crossed
toward the changed-object lane treated more naturally in the next chapter.

27.5.8     Stochastic and minibatch cautions
Stochastic or minibatch transport ideas are tempting because they reduce local work per
update [Genevay et al., 2016, 2019, Nguyen et al., 2022, 2021]. But a minibatch-optimal
plan is not automatically a valid full- ensemble deterministic resampling map. Solving
transport on sampled subclouds or local batches may be a useful approximation strategy,
yet the first question remains whether the resulting corrected route preserves the declared
teacher well enough on the full weighted ensemble.
    For this reason, minibatch variants belong to the retained-teacher lane only when a
later correction stage or explicit audit shows that full-ensemble marginals, transported-
cloud behavior, and downstream scalars still track the declared teacher route. The prac-
tical validation sequence should therefore stay stricter than a paper-summary reading:
 (1) first check small dense transported-particle parity, not only scalar OT values,
 (2) then check row and column marginals plus positivity/non-finite failures,
 (3) then inspect representation diagnostics such as rank, feature dimension, sparsity,
     projection count, or block locality,
 (4) only after value parity consider gradient smoke tests and larger- N, dx runtime or
     memory ladders,
 (5) and only after those local checks interpret downstream filtering evidence.
If the minibatch construction is instead promoted as its own randomized or local replace-
ment transport, it should be read through the later structure-changing chapters rather
than through the present retained-teacher one.

27.5.9       How the broader retained-teacher approximations fit here
The same residual logic gives the chapter a place to classify the broader scalable-OT
approximations from the survey. If a Nystrom factorization, a positive-feature kernel, or
a low-rank coupling factorization is proposed as a retained-teacher acceleration, then the
first audit question is still teacher preservation: how close is the transported cloud or
coupling application to the declared teacher route from Chapter 25?
    For example, a kernel-factor route may replace the dense Gibbs kernel by a factorized
approximation while still producing a coupling application of the same schematic form. A
low-rank coupling route may store and apply transport through structured factors rather
than a dense matrix. A stochastic or minibatch route may reduce computation by solving
smaller transport subproblems. In all such cases, this chapter’s doctrine is the same: they
are still retained-teacher candidates only if the approximation error is measured against
the teacher object rather than hidden behind speedups alone.
    That is why the residual hierarchy should be read broadly. The diagnostic is not
restricted to one neural warm-start map. It is the first reusable test for any approxima-
tion family that claims to accelerate the teacher without changing the meaning of the
transported output. Once the approximation stops being naturally judged by teacher-
preservation residuals, it belongs in the later target-changing chapters instead of this
retained-teacher one.



27.6       Filtering-loop insertion point
Inside the filtering loop, the retained-teacher neural route sits exactly where Chapter 25
placed the finite EOT/Sinkhorn layer:

                              student warm start+retained Sinkhorn
                 {xi , wi }N   −−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−−→ {x̃(j) , 1/N }N
                           i=1 −                                    j=1 .                    (27.45)

It accelerates the equal-weighting layer after the weighted cloud has already been formed.
It does not redefine the earlier particle-weighting rule itself.
27.7. VERIFICATION AND NON-CLAIMS                                                    265

27.7      Verification and non-claims
A practical implementation should still check a few local quantities carefully:

 (1) teacher generation is declared and reproducible,

 (2) the predicted latent teacher object is named explicitly,

 (3) the corrected route satisfies the row/column residual contract,

 (4) teacher-student cloud discrepancy remains below the declared threshold on the
     tested envelope,

 (5) the downstream scalar is checked whenever the learned route is embedded in a
     filtering likelihood or HMC target.

   These checks are mathematical and numerical, not bureaucratic. Their purpose is
only to ensure that the reader can tell whether the implementation is still computing the
declared teacher-student object or has drifted to a different one.
   This chapter does not claim:

    that the student replaces the teacher object,

    that small teacher-student residuals automatically imply posterior or HMC correct-
     ness,

    that broader neural OT families are unimportant, only that they answer a different
     implementation question.

Its role is narrower: fix one teacher-student acceleration route in a form that a reader
can nearly implement directly.
Chapter 28

ICNN, Brenier Maps, and
Monge-Gap Direct Map Learning

The previous chapter studied the narrowest neural extension of the entropic OT teacher:
retain the teacher and learn how to start its solver better. The present chapter changes
the question. Instead of accelerating a declared solver, it asks how one can learn the
transport map itself.
    This is a more ambitious route. The potential gain is obvious: if a good map is learned
directly, one may bypass repeated iterative solves at deployment time. The cost is equally
important: the learned object is no longer an initialization for a retained teacher. It is
the transport map itself, so every modeling and training choice now acts directly on the
output cloud.
    This chapter therefore has one dominant task: teach the reader what direct-map
learning is trying to learn, why Brenier/ICNN and Monge-gap methods are natural rep-
resentatives of that lane [Amos et al., 2017, Makkuva et al., 2020, Uscidda and Cuturi,
2023], and what evidence is needed once no corrective teacher solve remains in control.


28.1      What changes when the map itself is learned?
The best way to read this chapter is to compare it with the retained-teacher warm-start
chapter.

    In the warm-start chapter, the teacher still decides what the final transport plan
     and output cloud are; the learner only helps the teacher solve its own problem
     faster.

    In the present chapter, the learner itself proposes the transport map. There may
     be no corrective Sinkhorn phase at all.

So the central question is no longer “did we accelerate the same teacher?” It is “what
map object have we learned, and under what assumptions should we trust it?”


Plain-language takeaway. If the previous chapter was about helping an expensive
trusted calculation, this chapter is about replacing that calculation by a learned map.
That is why the mathematical structure and the evidence contract both change.

                                           266
28.2. RUNNING DIRECT-MAP CELL                                                        267

How to read the rest of this chapter. The sequence now splits into two direct-map
routes. First comes the Brenier/ICNN family, which keeps a strong structural prior by
learning a convex potential whose gradient defines the map. Then comes the Monge-gap
family, which keeps the same direct-map goal but relaxes the structural prior and asks
instead how OT-like the learned endpoint map remains under the chosen cost. Both
routes differ from the previous chapter in the same decisive way: there is no corrective
teacher solve standing behind the final output object.

28.3      Direct-map lane: object changed, evidence changed
A direct map-learning method tries to produce a deterministic transport map
                                       T : Rdx → Rdx .                                    (28.5)
The source measure µ and target measure ν are related by the pushforward relation
                                         T# µ = ν,                                        (28.6)
meaning that if one samples X ∼ µ and then computes T (X), the law of that transformed
sample is ν. Equivalently, for every test function f for which the integrals exist,
                         Z                     Z
                            f (y) d(T# µ)(y) = f (T (x)) dµ(x).                     (28.7)

At the empirical-cloud level, this means that if the chapter starts from source particles
xi ∼ µ and evaluates zi = T (xi ), then the mapped cloud {zi } is the finite-sample object
being asked to approximate the declared target law or target cloud.
   The important change relative to the warm-start chapter is immediate: the learned
object is no longer an internal solver coordinate. It is the transport map itself, or a
potential from which that map is derived. In the vocabulary of the OT block, retained-
teacher learning changes the execution path while a corrected solve still returns to a
declared transport object. Direct-map learning changes the transport object directly and
therefore inherits a different evidence contract.

28.4      Brenier viewpoint
In the quadratic-cost Euclidean setting, a classical route is to represent the map as the
gradient of a convex potential [Villani, 2003, Peyré and Cuturi, 2019, Vesseron and Cuturi,
2024]:
                             T ⋆ (x) = ∇ψ ⋆ (x),    ψ ⋆ convex.                      (28.8)

The quickest intuition is geometric. Quadratic-cost transport prefers maps with a mono-
tone or, more precisely, cyclically monotone structure. Gradients of convex potentials are
the canonical way to realize that structure. In one dimension this reduces to the familiar
monotone rearrangement picture: sort the mass from left to right and move it without
crossings. In higher dimension the theorem-strength statement is subtler, but the guiding
lesson is the same: the more the transport is forced to behave like a monotone gradient
field, the more a convex potential becomes a natural object to learn. This is why the
Brenier viewpoint appears so naturally: instead of learning an arbitrary map, learn a
scalar potential whose gradient already lives in a mathematically privileged map family.
    This statement should be read with its theorem-level assumptions attached. The
classical Brenier characterization is a continuous-measure result for quadratic cost in
Euclidean space under regularity conditions such as finite second moments and abso-
lute continuity of the source measure with respect to Lebesgue measure. In the finite
empirical-cloud setting used throughout BayesFilter, a Monge map may fail to exist or
fail to be unique in that theorem-strength sense. So the present chapter uses the Brenier
viewpoint primarily as structured motivation for a learned map family, not as a blanket
theorem that every finite cloud transport problem in the particle-filter setting is exactly
represented by a gradient of a convex potential.
    In one dimension, this means the derivative of the potential defines the map. For the
translation cell above, one convenient choice is

                                              1
                                     ψ ⋆ (x) = x2 + x.                               (28.9)
                                              2

Then
                                 ∇ψ ⋆ (x) = x + 1 = T ⋆ (x).                        (28.10)

The second derivative of ψ ⋆ is 1, so the potential is convex. This tiny calculation is the
cleanest way to see what the Brenier/ICNN family is trying to exploit: instead of learning
the map directly, it learns a structured potential whose gradient gives the map.
    A small finite-cloud warning is useful here. Even in tiny empirical problems, the
transport object may fail to be a single theorem-strength Monge map. If one source
atom of mass 1 must feed two target atoms of mass 1/2 each, the natural finite-cloud
transport may split mass across targets rather than assign one unique endpoint to that
source atom. This is exactly why the chapter treats Brenier as a structured motivation
ladder rather than as an automatic finite-cloud theorem.
270CHAPTER 28. ICNN, BRENIER MAPS, AND MONGE-GAP DIRECT MAP LEARNING

What survives from Brenier theory in this chapter. The theorem-strength Bre-
nier result is not being imported wholesale into the finite-cloud BayesFilter setting. What
survives here is a narrower bridge. The quadratic-cost theory says that convex-potential
gradients are a mathematically natural map family when the continuous assumptions
hold. The monograph then uses that fact as structured motivation for a direct-map
parameterization. What does not survive automatically is a theorem that every finite
empirical-cloud transport problem in this particle-filter setting is already solved exactly
by an ICNN potential. The reader should therefore carry forward a three-way separa-
tion: continuous-theorem support, structured finite-cloud motivation, and the separate
empirical question of whether the learned map behaves well once embedded in the actual
BayesFilter computation.


28.5      ICNN/Brenier route
Input-convex neural networks (ICNNs) provide a parametric family of scalar functions
that remain convex in designated inputs [Amos et al., 2017, Makkuva et al., 2020]. The
implementation idea is:

  (i) parameterize the potential ψ by an ICNN ψθ ,

 (ii) obtain the transport map by differentiating the network, Tθ (x) = ∇ψθ (x),

(iii) train ψθ so that the induced map sends source mass toward the target according to
      the chosen OT objective.

    The middle step is the important one to slow down. The learned object is not yet
a teacher-side coupling or a corrected barycentric cloud. It is the potential ψθ , together
with the gradient-defined endpoint map Tθ = ∇ψθ that later code will actually apply
to the source particles. So the training objective is not certifying “the same object as
the retained teacher, only faster.” It is certifying, at best, that this chosen map family
behaves plausibly under the declared direct-map evidence contract.
    A useful mathematical picture to keep in view is not one universal training formula,
but the structural relation
                               ψ ∗ (y) = sup{x⊤ y − ψ(x)},                          (28.11)
                                          x

between a convex potential and its convex conjugate. In theorem-strength quadratic-cost
OT, Brenier structure motivates learning a convex potential whose gradient gives the
map. In practical finite-cloud implementations, however, several objective families are
used: dual or conjugate-based objectives, empirical pushforward penalties, or regularized
map-learning surrogates. The present chapter therefore uses the Brenier/ICNN viewpoint
primarily as structured motivation for the map family, not as a claim that one displayed
objective automatically covers every finite-cloud training loop.
    One good way to read the displayed objective is to track the roles of its two functions
separately. The network parameter θ chooses the source-side potential ψθ , whose gradient
becomes the deployed map. The function φ plays the complementary target-side role: it
scores where the mapped samples land. For a fixed φ, however, the final expectation over
Y ∼ ν is constant in θ, so target information reaches the inner minimization only through
φ itself, not through that constant term. The formula is not saying that every direct-map
implementation literally fixes this φ in advance. It is saying that one common way to
28.5. ICNN/BRENIER ROUTE                                                                  271

train a Brenier-style map is to balance a source-to-map transport cost against a target-
side scoring term that rewards mapped samples for matching the intended target law.
For a practical reading, a first-year reader can think of φ as the target-side scoring object
in the objective: whether it is updated alternately or learned jointly depends on the exact
implementation. If it were held fixed, the inner problem would ignore ν entirely, so a
genuinely target-anchored trainer must include some φ-side update or a target-informed
choice of φ.
    The attraction of this route is that the map is not a black-box regressor. It is con-
strained to come from a convex potential, which is exactly the sort of structure the
quadratic-cost theory suggests under its stated assumptions.
    A concrete schematic training objective helps fix ideas. One representative potential-
based route is to choose a target-side potential φ and solve an objective of the schematic
form                                                        
                           1                 2
               min EX∼µ ∥X − ∇ψθ (X)∥ − φ(∇ψθ (X)) + EY ∼ν [φ(Y )].                    (28.12)
                 θ         2
This should not be read as the only ICNN objective in the literature. Its role in this
chapter is narrower: it makes explicit what one direct-map learner may optimize. The
first expectation penalizes the source-to-map transport cost while evaluating the target-
side potential on the mapped samples. The second expectation records the target-side
potential on samples from ν; for fixed φ it is constant in θ, so by itself it does not anchor
the inner minimization to ν. Target anchoring must come from how φ is chosen, updated,
or learned. At deployment time the object used by later code is still the gradient-defined
endpoint map Tθ = ∇ψθ , not the training objective itself. The display and algorithm
below are therefore a schematic direct-map training pattern, not a claim that one fully
specified canonical trainer has been derived in this chapter. A first-year reader should
therefore read the objective in four rungs:
  (i) choose a convex potential family ψθ ,
 (ii) obtain the endpoint map by differentiation,
(iii) optimize a loss built from mapped samples and target-side information,
 (iv) deploy only the resulting endpoint map, not the training loss itself.
   The cost is also immediate from the equations. One must evaluate gradients of the
potential and, depending on the chosen training formulation, may need to evaluate or
approximate conjugate or dual terms. So the route trades a retained transport solver for
a more structured but more delicate map-learning objective.

Reader checkpoint. Three evidential layers should remain separate for this route:
  (i) whether the learned map reaches the right endpoint law or cloud well enough,
 (ii) whether the learned map still behaves like a plausible OT-style map under the
      declared cost and structural prior,
(iii) whether a downstream scalar built from the mapped particles remains stable once
      this learned map is inserted into filtering or HMC-adjacent code.
A good training loss or good endpoint fit may support the first layer without yet settling
the second or third.

    tive

    directly into the parameterization
10: end while
11: On held-out validation clouds, compute mapped particles Tθ (xi )
12: Evaluate endpoint pushforward mismatch, transport-cost proxy, and downstream
    scalar sensitivity on the held-out clouds
13: Return ψθ , the induced map Tθ , and the declared diagnostics


Approximation enters here. The learned object is the transport map itself. Errors
in the learned potential or its gradient directly change the transported output cloud.

Why the next section changes emphasis rather than object. The Brenier/ICNN
route and the Monge-gap route are both direct-map answers. The learned endpoint map
is still the primary object in both cases. What changes in the next section is not the
endpoint ambition but the structural prior: instead of forcing the map to arise from one
especially rigid potential family, the chapter asks how to penalize a candidate map when
it behaves unlike an OT map under the chosen cost.


28.6      Monge-gap route
A more flexible direct-map family regularizes a candidate map by how far it behaves
from an OT map rather than forcing a particular architecture from the start [Uscidda
and Cuturi, 2023]. For cost c and reference measure ρ, the Monge gap is
                                Z
                         c
                      Mρ (T ) = c(x, T (x)) dρ(x) − Wc (ρ, T# ρ).             (28.13)

Here ρ is an explicitly declared reference measure used to probe how OT-like the learned
map is on the region of state space that matters for the intended application. In the
simplest reading one may take ρ = µ, so the regularizer is applied on the same source
measure used for transport. But a chapter, experiment, or implementation may instead
28.6. MONGE-GAP ROUTE                                                                   273

choose a different reference measure to emphasize a wider training envelope or a different
weighting of the state space. The role of ρ must therefore be named explicitly rather
than left implicit.
    The key structural property is immediate from the definition. The deterministic map
x 7→ T (x) induces a coupling between ρ and T# ρ, so by the definition of optimal transport,
                                           Z
                             Wc (ρ, T# ρ) ≤ c(x, T (x)) dρ(x).                       (28.14)

In slightly fuller words: the map-induced coupling γT = (Id, T )# ρ is one admissible
coupling between the source measure and the pushforward target. The optimal-transport
cost Wc (ρ, T# ρ) is the infimum over all admissible couplings with those same marginals,
so it cannot exceed the cost of this specific map-induced one. Therefore

                                       Mcρ (T ) ≥ 0,                                (28.15)

with equality when the map-induced coupling is already optimal for transporting ρ to
T# ρ. This is why the Monge gap is a meaningful regularizer: it measures how far the
learned map behaves from an OT map under the chosen cost.
    As a mathematical definition, the Monge gap is exact. But in a practical training
loop, the second term is typically not available in closed form because the pushforward
measure T# ρ itself depends on the current learned map. So the reader should picture a
four-step ladder:

  (i) define the exact Monge-gap quantity mathematically,

 (ii) recognize that the OT reference term is usually unavailable in closed form inside
      training,

(iii) replace that unavailable term by a declared estimator or surrogate,

(iv) interpret the resulting optimization only as strongly as that surrogate justification
     allows.

A concrete empirical surrogate is obtained by drawing reference samples xi ∼ ρ, forming
mapped particles zi = Tθ (xi ), and defining
                                  m                     m        m
                                                                     !
               cc (Tθ ) =      1 X                   1 X       1 X
              M   ρ,m               c(xi , zi ) − Wc      δx ,     δz .          (28.16)
                              m i=1                  m i=1 i m i=1 i

The second term is now a batchwise discrete OT problem on the empirical reference
cloud and its mapped image. This is now a finite-sample training quantity, not the exact
population Monge gap. So any finite-sample training objective that uses an estimated
OT reference term should be read as a surrogate or approximate Monge-gap objective
unless the estimator and its properties are stated explicitly. Operationally, the chapter’s
point is: fit a useful map, but penalize it when it behaves unlike an OT map for the
chosen cost. A useful mental model is that the training loop is differentiating through
two finite objects at once: the mapped sample cloud and a discrete OT computation
on that cloud. If either one is a poor proxy for the intended downstream use case, the
empirical Monge-gap objective may still decrease while the later filtering scalar drifts in
an undesired direction.
274CHAPTER 28. ICNN, BRENIER MAPS, AND MONGE-GAP DIRECT MAP LEARNING

    The running cell already shows the idea. The good and bad endpoint maps above
both match the endpoint law, but the bad map moves mass much less efficiently. On
that tiny example, the direct transport cost of the good map is 12 (12 + 12 ) = 1, while the
bad map has cost 21 (32 + 12 ) = 5. So even before worrying about population measures or
finite-sample estimators, the Monge-gap logic is already visible: two maps can fit the same
endpoint cloud while differing sharply in how OT-like their transport behavior is under
the chosen cost. The Monge-gap route is attractive precisely because it can discourage
such maps without forcing the full ICNN/Brenier structural commitment.

Algorithm 8 train monge gap regularized direct map

Reader checkpoint. The Monge-gap route still learns a direct map, but it relaxes the
strong ICNN-only structural commitment. The gain is flexibility. The cost is that the
learned map is now judged relative to a regularized OT-like behavior rather than by a
retained teacher solver.


28.7      Structured variants and boundaries
The same direct-map logic can be combined with additional structural priors, such as
sparse displacement or factorized transport structure [Forrow et al., 2019, Chen et al.,
2024, Xu et al., 2025, Geuter et al., 2025]. These are worth keeping in view because
they may be useful when the filtering update itself has a scientifically justified sparse
or low-active-subspace geometry. But they inherit the same chapter-wide burden: the
learned endpoint map itself must be validated, rather than interpreted through a retained
corrective teacher.
28.8. WHY THIS IS NOT THE DEFAULT FIRST ROUTE                                                 275

   This is why the direct-map route should be read as a different scalable-OT answer
from retained-teacher acceleration. It is more radical than teacher-preserving factorized
Sinkhorn, because the final map object itself is learned. But it is still narrower than the
dynamic or operator families of the next chapter, because it aims to learn one endpoint
map rather than an entire transport path or measure-level operator. The next chapter
therefore does not continue the same endpoint-map story at larger scale; it changes
the learned object again, from one final map to richer path, velocity-field, or operator
representations.

28.8       Why this is not the default first route
The direct-map families are mathematically serious and potentially powerful, but they
are not the monograph’s default first implementation route for two reasons:
  (i) they learn the final map object itself rather than only accelerating a declared teacher
      solve,

 (ii) their strongest mathematical support depends on more specific geometric assump-
      tions than the retained-teacher acceleration route requires.

28.8.1     Direct-map families as a different scalable-OT answer
The boundary with the retained-teacher chapter can be made even clearer. Nystrom,
positive-feature, and related entropic approximations begin by asking how to preserve
or approximate a declared teacher transport object more cheaply. The direct-map route
asks a different question: can one learn the final transport map itself well enough that
repeated teacher solves are no longer the center of the method?
    That difference is not merely architectural. It changes the meaning of the main
residual. In the retained-teacher lane, the first residual is naturally a teacher-preservation
discrepancy. In the direct-map lane, the primary residuals are pushforward mismatch,
Monge-gap behavior, transport-cost proxy, and scalar drift under the learned map. So
this chapter should be read as a target-boundary chapter: it explains why a direct-map
learner is not just “a stronger warm start,” but a new answer to the scalable-OT problem
with a different evidence contract.
    In practical terms, this chapter occupies the middle position between the retained-
teacher approximation lane and the broader replacement/dynamic lane. It is more radical
than teacher-preserving factorized Sinkhorn, because the map itself is learned. But it is
276CHAPTER 28. ICNN, BRENIER MAPS, AND MONGE-GAP DIRECT MAP LEARNING

still narrower than the dynamic/operator families of the next chapter, because it aims to
learn one endpoint map rather than an entire transport path or measure-level operator.


28.9       Verification and non-claims
A minimal implementation-facing reading of this chapter should distinguish:

    what map object is being fit,

    what assumptions justify that map family,

    what endpoint, pushforward, transport-cost, or Monge-gap residuals are measured,

    what downstream scalar drift is checked once the learned map is embedded in
     filtering or HMC-adjacent code.

    The practical residuals differ from the retained-teacher lane because no corrective
Sinkhorn phase is automatically present to return to a declared teacher object. So end-
point fit, pushforward mismatch, transport-cost proxy, Monge-gap proxy, and down-
stream scalar sensitivity are part of the primary evidence, not side diagnostics.
    This chapter does not claim:

    that direct learned maps are interchangeable with retained-teacher EOT accelera-
     tion,

    that a map-level fit automatically preserves the same filtering scalar,

    that broader direct-map families are already validated for BayesFilter.

Its role is to slow down the direct-map family itself so the reader can see that it is solving
a different problem from the previous chapter.

Dynamic Geodesic and Operator
Learners, and the Filtering Target
Contract

The previous chapter treated direct map-learning families such as ICNN/Brenier and
Monge-gap approaches. The present chapter changes the learned object again. Instead
of asking the network to learn one static transport map, it asks what happens when the
learned object is a dynamic transport path, a velocity field, or an operator acting on
families of measures.
    This chapter is intentionally secondary. Its job is not to become another core im-
plementation chapter. Its job is to explain why these broader learned families carry an
even heavier target-status burden than retained-teacher acceleration or static direct-map
learning.


29.1      What changes when the learned object becomes
          richer?
The easiest way to read this chapter is to keep the following contrast in mind.

    The retained-teacher neural chapter learned how to solve a declared transport
     teacher faster.

    The direct-map chapter learned one final transport map.

    This chapter asks what happens when the learned object is richer than one final
     map: a path, a velocity field, or an operator on entire families of measures.

    So the main burden is not just implementation difficulty. The chapter’s stable question
is narrower and more useful:

     If the learned object is richer than one endpoint map, what scalar is down-
     stream code actually using, and what gradient interpretation still remains
     justified?

For the rest of this chapter, the recurring OT-block terms should be read in one stable
way:

    “target-changing” means the learned object is no longer automatically that same
     reference transport object,

    “same-scalar parity” means the reported gradient must differentiate the exact scalar
     value that is actually built from the learned object used by the code.

reduces the learned transport output into one value, either from the terminal cloud alone

29.2      Running path-versus-map example
A tiny one-dimensional toy example makes the distinction concrete. Suppose the source
cloud is
                                   Xsrc = {−1, 1}
and the target cloud is
                                        Xtgt = {0, 2}.
29.2. RUNNING PATH-VERSUS-MAP EXAMPLE                                                   279

A static-map learner tries to learn one rule such as

                                         T (x) = x + 1,                              (29.1)

which moves the source points directly to the target points.
    A dynamic path learner instead tries to describe how the particles move as a function
of pseudo-time λ ∈ [0, 1]. Two simple paths with the same endpoint map are

                     xA (λ) = x + λ,                              0 ≤ λ ≤ 1,         (29.2)
                     xB (λ) = x + λ2 ,                            0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.         (29.3)

Both paths satisfy

                 xA (0) = xB (0) = x,       xA (1) = xB (1) = x + 1 = T (x).

So they agree on the final endpoint transformation. But they disagree as soon as later
code cares about more than the endpoint. For example,

                                     Φmid (x(·)) = x(1/2)                            (29.4)

gives
                      Φmid (xA ) = x + 1/2,         Φmid (xB ) = x + 1/4,
and the path-action functional
                                              Z 1
                                 A(x(·)) =          |ẋ(λ)|2 dλ                      (29.5)
                                               0

produces                                              Z 1
                                                                   4
                       A(xA ) = 1,        A(xB ) =       (2λ)2 dλ = .
                                                       0           3
Thus two learned objects can agree on the endpoint map while still inducing different
path-dependent scalars.
    This distinction matters because later code need not use only the endpoint. At the
level of notation, the endpoint map in both examples is still

                                   T (x) = x(1) = x + 1,                             (29.6)

but a path-dependent scalar may instead use the whole trajectory x(·). For a BayesFilter-
style reading, imagine a scalar that averages only the terminal mapped particles versus
a scalar that also penalizes path action or an intermediate position. Those two scalars
may agree on the same endpoint map while still producing different values and different
gradients because they consume fundamentally different learned objects. Once intermedi-
ate positions, path functionals, or operator outputs enter the scalar that is differentiated
downstream, two learners with the same endpoint map can still define different effective
targets.

Plain-language takeaway. A richer learned transport object can preserve the same
endpoint while changing what downstream code means by the value and gradient it
consumes.
280CHAPTER 29. DYNAMIC GEODESIC AND OPERATOR LEARNERS, AND THE FILTERING T

29.3      Richer-object audit: endpoint, path, scalar, gra-
          dient
The toy example motivates the general audit ladder. Once the learned object is richer
than one endpoint map, the reader should slow down and ask three separate questions:
what object is being learned, what scalar later code builds from that object, and what
gradient can therefore be interpreted.

Object inventory. A dynamic transport learner no longer tries only to produce one
final map T . Instead it may try to learn:

    a geodesic path ρλ between source and target measures,

    a velocity field vλ (x) generating that path,

    or an operator G that maps input measures to output trajectories, output measures,
     or transport-related latent coordinates.

This is a larger algorithmic change because the learned object is no longer merely a
replacement endpoint map. It is a representation of how transport unfolds or how an
entire family of transport problems is parameterized.

What downstream code may consume. Once a richer object is available, later code
may consume:

    only the terminal map or endpoint cloud,

    intermediate positions or path summaries,

    action, regularity, or trajectory penalties,

    or operator outputs that vary across a family of related problems.

The object question therefore comes first. One cannot decide what scalar is being com-
puted until one knows what learned object the scalar is built from.

Same-scalar warning. The most important target-contract warning survives every
change of learned object. If a downstream routine uses a scalar L    e built from a learned
map, path, or operator, then the reported gradient must differentiate that same scalar.
Even if this value-gradient parity holds, the result is coherent only for the learned target
unless a correction returns to the teacher or original target.

Same-scalar template. The chapter’s main interpretive contract can be written schemat-
ically as
                   Oθ 7−→ L
                          eθ = Φ(Oθ ; data),    gθ = ∇θ Leθ ,                 (29.7)
where Oθ is the learned object (map, path, or operator output), L     eθ is the actual down-
stream scalar built from that object, and gθ is the reported gradient. A concrete BayesFilter-
style example to keep in mind is a scalar that averages a terminal equal-weight cloud
before passing it into a later filtering reduction. If a richer learner instead contributes a
path penalty or an operator-generated summary to that scalar, then the object feeding Φ
29.4. DYNAMIC GEODESIC LEARNERS                                                              281

has changed even if the endpoint cloud looks similar. The gradient is interpretable only if
it differentiates that same declared scalar built from that same learned object. Even per-
fect value-gradient parity therefore certifies coherence only for the learned target unless
a correction returns to the earlier teacher.

29.4       Dynamic geodesic learners
Some neural OT papers learn Wasserstein geodesics or associated velocity fields [Hanebeck,
2023, Gracyk and Chen, 2024, Liu and Chen, 2026]. The minimal mathematical picture
is that a dynamic transport object is no longer only an endpoint map T . It is a pseudo-
time path of measures (ρλ )0≤λ≤1 together with a velocity field vλ (x) satisfying a continuity
equation of the schematic form

                                   ∂λ ρλ + ∇ · (ρλ vλ ) = 0,                              (29.8)

with endpoints
                                      ρ0 = µ,      ρ1 = ν.                                (29.9)
In a Benamou–Brenier-style reading, one then judges a path by a transport-action objec-
tive of the schematic form    Z Z     1
                                          ∥vλ (x)∥2 dρλ (x) dλ.                          (29.10)
                                  0
The endpoint map is now only one summary of a richer learned object; the path and
velocity field are themselves part of what later code could use.
    This is mathematically appealing because particle-flow filtering already has a pseudo-
time flavor. The attraction is therefore obvious: perhaps one could learn reusable trans-
port dynamics instead of solving a fresh static problem each time.
    The caution is equally important. A dynamic geodesic learner does not answer the
same question as a retained finite Sinkhorn solver. It learns a richer object and must
therefore be judged against a richer scalar-and-gradient interpretation. The first audit
question is not merely whether the endpoint fit is good. It is whether the downstream
scalar is built from the same path object whose gradient is later reported.

to make the richer learned object concrete, not to promote dynamic-path learning as the
monograph’s default BayesFilter implementation route.

29.5       Operator learners
A related family learns operators on spaces of measures [Lu et al., 2021, Li et al., 2021,
Kovachki et al., 2023]. In such approaches, the input is itself a measure or empirical
cloud, and the output is either another measure, a path of measures, or a set of latent
coordinates describing the transport. A useful empirical-cloud signature is

   Gθ : (µ, context) 7−→ endpoint cloud, path object, or transport latent state.      (29.11)

Concretely, one may imagine an operator that takes an empirical cloud together with
problem context and returns a terminal transformed cloud, a whole pseudo-time path,
or transport-related latent coordinates for a family of related filtering problems. For
example, one operator might take a weighted particle cloud together with observation
context and output a full pseudo-time path whose terminal state is then reduced into a
filtering scalar. Another might output only a terminal cloud. The chapter’s point is that
these two outputs can induce different scalars and therefore different gradient meanings
even when they start from the same input ensemble. In that sense, the operator section
should be read as the family-level analogue of the earlier path-vs-endpoint toy example:
the repeated scalar L  e is still the anchor, but the object fed into it has changed.
     The main conceptual advantage is reuse across families of problems. The main concep-
tual cost is that the learned object is now even less tied to one declared teacher solve. So
the first question is no longer only “does this recover one finite teacher route well enough?”
It is “what family-level target is this operator inducing across the class of problems to
which it is applied?” That makes these methods valuable as research-direction chapters,
but not as the default first implementation route in this monograph.
29.6. TARGET-CHANGING BOUNDARY FAMILIES                                                283

29.6       Target-changing boundary families
Several important high-dimensional families fit this chapter because they should not be
read as compressed dense-teacher solvers by default. The common theme is simple: they
may still produce useful transport surrogates, but the object they compute is no longer
automatically the same full-state dense transport object that earler chapters treated as
the reference lane.

Projected families: sliced and subspace OT. Sliced and subspace OT methods

fact is one-dimensional OT itself. For one-dimensional measures, the monotone transport
map is

reconstructed transport object is now acting on the filtering ensemble. In the running toy
spirit, the key contrast is: the reference lane earlier in the OT block acted through one
full-state transport object, whereas a sliced route acts through many lower-dimensional
projected ones whose average or reconstruction must still be interpreted with care. If
the recurring scalar Le is built from those projected outputs, then the gradient is only a
gradient of that projected-object scalar, not automatically of the earlier dense reference
scalar.

29.6.1     Sliced, subspace, and localization families as target-changing
           lanes
The scalable-OT survey gives this chapter a more precise boundary around several impor-
tant high-dimensional families. Sliced and subspace OT methods attack high dimension
by projecting the measures onto one-dimensional directions or selected subspaces before
solving lower-dimensional transport problems. Localization and block-structured OT in-
stead exploit state-space structure by transporting local blocks or using localized costs
rather than one global cloud-wide coupling.
    These methods are mathematically important, but in the BayesFilter monograph they
should not be described as mere compressed versions of the dense entropic teacher. A
projected one-dimensional or subspace transport, or a block-localized transport, is gen-
erally a different transport object from the full-state dense coupling used in the previous
chapters. That means the main burden here is target interpretation rather than just
solver engineering.
    In that sense, sliced/subspace and localization families fit the present chapter better
than the retained-teacher chapter. Their primary promise is not simply to reach the
same teacher object faster. Their promise is to define a more tractable transport rule in
high dimension. The price is that the resulting output cloud must usually be read as a
new resampling approximation unless a separate argument shows how the projected or
localized transport reconstructs the intended full-state object.
    This chapter therefore treats these families as target-changing or structure-changing
candidates by default. They may still be useful and even necessary in high dimension,
but their first audit question is no longer only teacher-preservation residual. It is: what
transport object is now being applied to the filtering ensemble, and what scalar target
would a later optimizer or HMC routine actually differentiate if this object were embedded
downstream?

Structured families: localization and block transport. Localization and block-
structured OT instead exploit state-space structure by transporting local blocks or using
localized costs rather than one global cloud- wide coupling. A schematic block decompo-
sition is
                                           (1)         (B)

The first option says: transport each block with its own local rule. The second says: keep
one particle-level coupling, but define that coupling through a cost that is itself localized
across scientifically meaningful state blocks. In plain language, the computed object
may therefore be a structured local transport rule rather than one dense global coupling.
This can be scientifically sensible when the state decomposition itself is justified, but
it still changes the object whose scalar consequences downstream code will inherit. So
29.7. SAME-SCALAR RULE REVISITED                                                        285

the reader must ask not only whether the method is faster or more stable, but which
structured transport object is actually being applied and what stronger dense-parity
claim is therefore no longer automatic.

Boundary markers only. Several additional families remain useful only as boundary
markers here: measure-to-measure regression operators, local Wasserstein regression, and
manifold or Riemannian neural OT [Vandergrift et al., 2026, Girshfeld and Chen, 2025,
Micheli et al., 2026]. They show how quickly the learned object can drift from the
current finite-cloud Euclidean teacher, but they do not by themselves answer the present
implementation question.


29.7      Same-scalar rule revisited
What the remaining sections now do. The previous sections identified richer fami-
lies by the object they learn and by how quickly that object can drift away from the earlier
dense reference route. The remaining sections do not introduce new families. They in-
stead collect the audit questions that help the reader decide what interpretation remains
mathematically supported once the learned object is richer than a static endpoint map.

Mini audit example. Suppose a learner reports a gradient for a scalar that uses both
the terminal cloud and the path-action penalty from the running example. If the code
used to compute the scalar includes A(x(·)) but the reported gradient differentiates only
the terminal map T (x) = x(1), then same-scalar parity has failed even if the endpoint
cloud looks correct. The strongest justified interpretation in that case is only that the
endpoint map is reasonable as a transport summary; it is not that the reported gradient is
the derivative of the actual executed scalar. The same logic applies to operator learners
and projected/localized families: once the filtering-style scalar uses the richer object,
the audit must stay tied to that same object all the way through value and gradient
evaluation.


29.8      How to audit a richer learned object
For richer learned objects, a few mathematical consistency checks are especially impor-
tant:
  (i) whether endpoint or pathwise improvement is accompanied by stability of the down-
      stream scalar,
 (ii) whether the learned object behaves robustly under weight, dimension, or particle-
      count shift,
(iii) whether a reported gradient is the gradient of the same scalar value that is later
      interpreted downstream,
(iv) whether any claim of target preservation is supported by an explicit correction
     mechanism rather than by smoothness or speed alone.
These are not governance gates. They are simply the mathematical checks needed to
understand what object is being computed, what scalar is built from that object, and
what interpretation remains identifiable from the reported gradient.

Reader checkpoint. This procedure does not approve or reject a method in an insti-
tutional sense. It simply organizes the chapter’s local question: what object was learned,
what scalar was built from it, and what gradient interpretation is still justified for that
same scalar?



29.9      Relation to the full HMC target chapter
This chapter stops at the target-status burden created by broader dynamic and operator
learners. It does not settle the HMC question. That full taxonomy still belongs to Chap-
ter 30, which interprets the scalar and gradient contracts rung by rung across the whole
DPF ladder. Put more sharply: the present chapter settles the local object-identification
question, while the later HMC chapter settles the broader sampler-interpretation ques-
tion.


OT-block takeaway. The OT sequence has now split into three broad implementa-
tion postures. The entropic OT chapter fixed the semantics-preserving reference lane.
The retained- teacher chapter kept that object but learned how to reach it faster. The
direct- map and dynamic/operator chapters then moved into target-changing territory
by learning endpoint maps, paths, or measure-level operators directly. The next HMC
and debugging chapters therefore do not ask which family is most elegant in the abstract;
they ask what scalar each family induces and what evidence is needed before any stronger
claim is made.
29.10. WHAT THIS CHAPTER DOES AND DOES NOT CLAIM                                       287

29.10       What this chapter does and does not claim
This chapter explains why the broadest neural OT families should be read as secondary
research directions in this monograph. It does not claim:

    that geodesic, operator, and adjacent measure/manifold families solve the same
     implementation problem as retained-teacher acceleration,

    that a richer learned object is automatically more useful for BayesFilter,

    that these families are already ready for the same implementation status as the
     earlier chapters.

Its role is to close the learned-transport part responsibly by keeping the broadest learned
families in view while handing the full target-status question forward to the HMC inter-
pretation and verification chapters.

 HMC Target Interpretation,

Chapter 30

DPF HMC Target Correctness and
Structural-Model Suitability

The preceding particle, transport, and learned-surrogate chapters built a ladder of in-
creasingly differentiable filtering constructions: raw particle-flow proposals, proposal-
corrected PF-PF, soft differentiable resampling, deterministic OT equal-weighting, en-
tropic optimal-transport relaxation with Sinkhorn, custom-gradient LEDH-PFPF-OT
differentiation for the declared finite value path, retained-teacher learned transport ac-
celeration, and broader learned-map or dynamic-transport surrogates. This chapter asks
a narrower and more severe question. If one of those constructions is used inside Hamil-
tonian Monte Carlo for a nonlinear DSGE or MacroFinance model, what target is the
Markov chain intended to leave invariant?
    The answer cannot be inferred from the label “differentiable particle filter.” HMC
is a target-specific algorithm. Its mathematical interpretation depends on the scalar log
target used for accept/reject decisions, the gradient used by the numerical integrator,
and the correction mechanism, if any [Neal, 2011, Betancourt, 2017]. Particle MCMC
adds a separate target logic: an unbiased, nonnegative likelihood estimator can define
a corrected extended-space chain under pseudo-marginal assumptions, but that is not
the same object as a smooth surrogate likelihood differentiated by HMC [Andrieu and
Roberts, 2009, Andrieu et al., 2010]. The DPF ladder must therefore separate three
questions:

  (i) whether the scalar value supplied to HMC is the intended posterior value, an unbi-
      ased estimator inside a corrected construction, or a deliberately approximate value;

 (ii) whether the gradient supplied to the integrator is the derivative of that same scalar
      value;

(iii) whether the evidence is strong enough for exploratory, research, or broader external
      claims.


30.1      Objects in the HMC target contract
Let θ ∈ Θ be the structural parameter and let u ∈ Rdθ be the unconstrained parameter
used by the sampler, with transform θ = T (u). Let

                ℓ(u) = log p(T (u)) + log L(y1:T | T (u)) + log |det DT (u)|

is exact. This expression assumes that the transform is differentiable on the sampler-

more general. In a DPF construction the likelihood term may be replaced by a particle,
relaxed, or learned object. The HMC contract is therefore stated for the actual scalar
value ℓ⋆ (u) used by the sampler, not for the method family name.

    Assume that ℓ⋆ : Rdθ → R is differentiable on the interior of the sampler’s valid
region, and that g : Rdθ → Rdθ is the vector field supplied to the integrator in the same
coordinates. The mass matrix M in the ordinary separable Hamiltonian is a symmetric
positive-definite dθ × dθ matrix, so p⊤ M −1 p is well defined. The minimum value-gradient
30.2. TARGET-STATUS TAXONOMY                                                            291

consistency condition is
                                     g(u) = ∇u ℓ⋆ (u).                               (30.1)
Equation (30.1) is not a claim that ℓ⋆ is the exact nonlinear filtering likelihood. It
is a claim that the gradient used by the integrator and the value used by the target
interpretation are the same mathematical object.
     If the value is ℓ⋆ but the integrator uses a vector field g ̸= ∇ℓ⋆ , the usual leapfrog
derivation no longer describes the Hamiltonian flow of H⋆ . A Metropolis correction may
still be valid for an arbitrary proposal only after reversibility, volume preservation, and
the correct acceptance ratio have been established. Without that separate proposal-level
proof, a smooth chain with mismatched value and gradient is not evidence of correct
HMC. If both value and gradient are changed to a relaxed or learned scalar, then the
chain may be internally coherent, but the target has changed to π⋆ .


30.2      Target-status taxonomy
The DPF chapters use the following target-status categories. The categories are delib-
erately conservative because a reviewer should be able to tell exactly what posterior,
extended posterior, or surrogate posterior is being discussed.

Exact-likelihood HMC
              HMC evaluates a deterministic scalar log posterior and its exact or au-
              dited derivative. Numerical integration error is corrected by the standard
              Metropolis step, provided the implemented proposal satisfies the usual
              HMC reversibility and volume-preservation assumptions.

Pseudo-marginal MCMC
            A random nonnegative likelihood estimator is included as part of an
            extended-space target. The claim is not that the estimator is a smooth
            likelihood surrogate. The claim is that marginal correctness follows from
            the pseudo-marginal construction under its assumptions [Andrieu and
            Roberts, 2009, Andrieu et al., 2010].

Noisy-gradient method
             A stochastic or approximate gradient is used to move the chain. This is
             not exact HMC unless a valid correction theory is stated. It may be useful
             as an optimization, adaptation, or diagnostic device, but that usefulness
             does not by itself identify the invariant posterior.

Delayed-acceptance or surrogate-corrected MCMC
             A surrogate or particle object proposes, screens, or accelerates moves,
             but a later correction evaluates the intended target. The target claim
             belongs to the corrected chain, not to the surrogate alone.

Relaxed-target HMC
             The scalar log target deliberately replaces a discontinuous or discrete
             filtering operation by a smooth relaxed operation, such as soft resampling
             or entropic OT. HMC can be coherent for this scalar if Equation (30.1)
             holds, but the posterior is the relaxed posterior.
292CHAPTER 30. DPF HMC TARGET CORRECTNESS AND STRUCTURAL-MODEL SUITABILI

Learned-surrogate HMC
             A neural or amortized map defines part of the scalar value. The chain
             targets the learned scalar only if value and gradient are consistent. It
             targets the original or teacher posterior only after a separate correction
             or error-bound argument strong enough for that claim.


30.3      Rung-by-rung target analysis
30.3.1     EDH and LEDH flow proposals
At the raw EDH or LEDH rung, the value object is a flow-based approximate filtering
quantity. The flow is derived from Gaussian closure or local linearization assumptions
and is integrated numerically. If HMC differentiates the same scalar flow object that it
evaluates, then the construction can satisfy value-gradient consistency for that scalar. Its
target status is nevertheless limited:

    exact-target HMC only in recovery cases where the flow construction equals the
     exact filtering likelihood, such as the linear-Gaussian benchmark;

    approximate-target or value-side benchmark HMC outside those recovery cases;

    diagnostic-only use if the implementation differentiates a path that differs from the
     scalar value used for accept/reject.

Smoothness of the flow ODE, by itself, does not upgrade a closure-based filtering approx-
imation into an exact nonlinear posterior target.


30.3.2     PF-PF proposal correction
At the PF-PF rung, the flow is used as a proposal and the scalar value includes the
proposal-to-target correction through importance weights and change-of-variables terms.
This is the first rung in the BayesFilter DPF ladder with an explicit proposal-correction
interpretation. That statement is not a production or validation claim. It means only
that the value-side target story is more defensible than raw flow transport because the
proposal density, Jacobian or log determinant, and particle weight enter the same scalar
object. The improvement is proposal-accounting clarity for the stated one-step condi-
tional construction in Chapter 22; it is not evidence, by itself, of multi-step posterior
fidelity, finite-particle stability, or HMC correctness.
    For HMC, the required scalar is the corrected particle objective actually used by the
sampler. The required gradient is the derivative of that same corrected objective, in-
cluding every differentiable term in the proposal density, transition density, measurement
density, flow map, and log determinant. The remaining evidence burden is substantial:

    finite-particle variability must be measured rather than hidden by a deterministic
     seed;

    log-determinant and Jacobian paths must be audited against the same value path;

    flow discretization error must be separated from Monte Carlo error;
30.3. RUNG-BY-RUNG TARGET ANALYSIS                                                      293

    compiled repeated evaluation must remain finite and reproducible on the structural
     model class being claimed;

    if randomness enters the HMC target, the construction must state whether it is
     pseudo-marginal extended-space MCMC, a fixed-randomness deterministic approx-
     imation, or a noisy-gradient diagnostic.

Thus PF-PF is a plausible first research rung for DPF-HMC experiments, not a full
HMC-validity theorem and not by itself a stronger external claim.


30.3.3     Soft differentiable resampling
Soft resampling replaces categorical ancestor selection by a differentiable mixture or
shrinkage construction [Zhu et al., 2020, Jonschkowski et al., 2018, Karkus et al., 2018].
The scalar value is therefore a soft-resampling filtering value. If HMC differentiates ex-
actly that scalar, the resulting chain can be internally coherent for the soft target. It
should not be described as sampling the categorical-resampling posterior unless a separate
correction is supplied.
    The core mathematical issue is nonlinear test-function bias. Even if a soft-resampling
map preserves a weighted mean under special conditions, it does not generally preserve
expectations of nonlinear functions, path genealogies, or the likelihood contribution of
the original categorical particle filter. The HMC label must therefore be relaxed-target
HMC, surrogate-target HMC, or diagnostic use, depending on the scalar value actually
corrected by the sampler.


30.3.4     OT and entropic OT resampling
At the OT/EOT rung, resampling is written as a transport problem [Reich, 2013, Cuturi,
2013, Peyré and Cuturi, 2019, Corenflos et al., 2021]. Entropic regularization and a finite
Sinkhorn solve make the construction differentiable and numerically structured, but they
also define a different map from exact categorical resampling. The scalar value must
specify the cost, entropy convention, regularization parameter, stopping tolerance, and
whether the unrolled solver path or an implicit derivative is used.
    The scalable-OT survey sharpens the target-status split inside this rung. Exact online
or streamed Sinkhorn implementations can still belong to the same relaxed entropic target
class if they preserve the same declared teacher object and the same executed scalar.
Their main changes are engineering changes in storage, blocking, or GPU execution, not
changes in the target definition itself. By contrast, factorized kernel routes, low-rank
coupling routes, sliced/subspace transports, and localized/block transports should not
all inherit that same status automatically. Some remain best read as retained-teacher
approximations, while others are better read as explicit new transport rules.
    For HMC, the target status is relaxed-target HMC when the accept/reject value and
gradient both use the same EOT/Sinkhorn scalar. Finite solver residuals, underflow
handling, stabilization, and ε sensitivity are target diagnostics, not mere implementation
details. A finite Sinkhorn layer does not become an exact categorical resampling layer
because its gradient exists. Nor does a faster implementation become a new target simply
because its execution path is different, provided the same scalar and same transport object
are still being evaluated.
294CHAPTER 30. DPF HMC TARGET CORRECTNESS AND STRUCTURAL-MODEL SUITABILI

30.3.5     Learned or amortized OT
Learned OT introduces a second approximation layer: a neural or amortized map is
trained to imitate, accelerate, or residual-correct a transport teacher [Amos et al., 2017,
Makkuva et al., 2020, Uscidda and Cuturi, 2023, Gracyk and Chen, 2024]. The scalar
value is then the learned scalar unless a correction evaluates the teacher or original target.
The gradient path is the derivative through the learned map and any explicitly retained
teacher terms.
     The scalable-OT survey helps separate two cases that should not be conflated. Retained-
teacher accelerators, such as warm-start predictors or other teacher-preserving approx-
imations, may still be judged first against the same transport teacher object. Their
HMC burden is therefore to show that the value and gradient are consistent for the same
learned-or-corrected scalar and that teacher-preservation residuals are understood on the
tested envelope. Broader transport learners, sliced or localized replacement rules, and
dynamic/operator families do not even begin with that teacher-preservation presumption.
They are better read as learned or replacement targets unless a separate correction or
error argument returns the chain to the teacher or original target.
     The target-status label must therefore be learned-surrogate HMC unless the imple-
mentation supplies a valid correction or an error analysis strong enough to promote the
claim. Runtime reduction, smoothness, and low teacher residual on training clouds are not
target-correctness evidence. The missing validation includes out-of-distribution particle-
cloud tests, seed sensitivity, posterior comparison against the EOT teacher, and stress
tests on structural parameter regions that are invalid, nearly invalid, or geometrically
stiff.

30.5       Pseudo-marginal and surrogate distinctions
The pseudo-marginal result and the DPF surrogate story are often confused because both

involve particle approximations. They are different claims. Suppose L(y

                                     h          i
                                       b | θ, ω) = L(y | θ).

Pseudo-marginal MCMC targets an extended density involving ω and can recover the
exact marginal posterior under its assumptions. The validity argument is an extended-
target argument. It is not an argument that log L b is a smooth deterministic likelihood
whose pathwise gradient is the gradient of log L.
    By contrast, a relaxed DPF target usually chooses a deterministic or fixed-randomness
scalar ℓ⋆ (θ) and differentiates it. HMC may be valid for ℓ⋆ if the value-gradient contract
and proposal correction hold. That does not imply validity for the original posterior ℓ(θ).
A delayed-acceptance or surrogate-corrected scheme can bridge the gap only if the final
correction evaluates the intended target with the right acceptance probability.

30.6      Why nonlinear DSGE models sharpen the issue
Nonlinear DSGE models make target drift especially costly because the filtering law is
tied to structural economics rather than only to a generic latent-state transition. The
DPF chapter does not need to solve the economics, but it must not hide target changes
inside a numerical method. The main DSGE stress points are:
  (i) Determinacy and invalid regions: the sampler will propose parameters outside
      or near determinacy regions. The target must return a declared finite penalty or
      −∞ policy, not an uncaught solver failure.
 (ii) Pruning and approximation convention: first-order, higher-order, pruned, and
      simulation-based approximations can define different latent laws. A DPF likelihood
      is only meaningful after the structural law is fixed.
(iii) Structural timing: observables, controls, states, and shocks must enter the tran-
      sition and measurement equations with the intended timing. A smooth filter for
      the wrong timing is still the wrong target.
(iv) Latent-state semantics: deterministic-completion coordinates and stochastic state
     coordinates are not interchangeable. Particle clouds must represent the declared
     latent law.
 (v) Local Jacobian fragility: EDH, LEDH, and proposal-corrected flow methods
     inherit local-linearization and derivative fragility near boundaries or stiff regions.
    For DSGE work, the correct conclusion is conservative. A DPF rung may be a useful
research target after it states its scalar value and diagnostics. It is not bank-facing evi-
dence until the structural law, invalid-region policy, value-gradient parity, and posterior
sensitivity have been tested on the named model class.


30.7      Why MacroFinance models sharpen the issue
MacroFinance latent-factor systems create a different target-risk profile. Their long pan-
els can amplify small likelihood changes, and their latent factors often interact with
volatility, measurement noise, and missing-data patterns. A relaxed or learned resam-
pling map that looks harmless on a short toy filter can move posterior mass materially
in a long panel.
    The minimum MacroFinance limitations to record are:
    latent dimension and particle degeneracy pressure;
    long observation spans that compound small per-period target changes;
    missing, ragged-edge, or mixed-frequency observation patterns;
    volatility and measurement-noise directions with sharp curvature;
    compiled repeatability across seeds, batches, and hardware settings;
    model-risk governance, including reproducible artifacts and claim boundaries.
These limitations do not rule out DPF research. They rule out treating a smooth dif-
ferentiable filtering path as operational-claim evidence before the target and validation
ladder have been passed.
30.8. RELATION TO SURROGATE-HMC ACCELERATION                                            297

30.8      Relation to surrogate-HMC acceleration
Surrogate-HMC and Hamiltonian-neural-network ideas address a different point in the
inference stack [Greydanus et al., 2019, Dhulipala et al., 2022, Hoffman et al., 2019, Parno
and Marzouk, 2018]. Chapter 51 gives the complete construction, proves the discrete
proposal conditions, and explains why a true endpoint likelihood value is not by itself a
universal correction. These methods attempt to improve movement through an already
chosen target, or to use a surrogate proposal that is later corrected against that target.
DPF methods may instead alter the filtering likelihood itself through flow approximation,
relaxed resampling, or learned transport. The distinction is operational:

    a corrected surrogate-HMC proposal can preserve the intended target if the correc-
     tion evaluates that target and the proposal assumptions hold;

    a relaxed DPF likelihood defines a new target unless a correction returns to the
     original likelihood;

    a learned DPF transport map defines a learned target unless the sampler corrects
     against the teacher or original target.

30.9       Evidence ladder for stronger external language

    No rung in this chapter is promoted to an operational claim. The strongest current
recommendation is a bounded experimental hypothesis: prioritize proposal-corrected PF-

then compare relaxed and learned rungs as deliberately changed targets. The hypoth-
