Chapter 43

Mass Matrices and Local Geometry

Mass matrices translate derivative information into sampler geometry. In a linear Gaus-
sian validation problem, a local posterior Hessian or observed information matrix can be
a useful preconditioner. In a nonlinear or weakly identified model, the same matrix can
be misleading unless it is regularized and checked against diagnostics.


43.1       Sources of Curvature
BayesFilter recognizes several curvature sources:

    analytic likelihood Hessian plus prior curvature;

    observed-information or expected-information approximations;

    finite-difference Hessian diagnostics at a MAP point;

    empirical covariance from warmup draws;

    diagonal fallbacks when dense curvature is unstable.

The source must be recorded because each source has a different failure mode. MacroFi-
nance mass-matrix tests check eigenvalue regularization, dense versus diagonal choices,
whitening finiteness, and covariance construction from Hessian helpers. These are geom-
etry utilities; they are not identification proofs.


43.2       Regularization Policy
A mass matrix used by HMC must be symmetric positive definite. If a curvature estimate
is indefinite or ill-conditioned, BayesFilter should regularize it, record the regularization,
and expose the eigenvalue diagnostics. Silently using an indefinite curvature matrix as if
it were a covariance is a target geometry error.


43.3       Geometry-Scaled Tuning Budgets
Mass-matrix diagnostics can inform preparation budgets. A fixed number of samples is
a policy choice, not a property of the model. BayesFilter’s geometry summary records:

                                             445
446                       CHAPTER 43. MASS MATRICES AND LOCAL GEOMETRY

       parameter dimension d;

       covariance condition number, when available;

       effective dimension, computed from the covariance eigenvalue spectrum;

       anisotropy ratio d/deff ;

       regularization pressure, including eigenvalue clipping, non-positive raw eigenvalues,
        and diagonal fallback use.

    Historical stage schedules use this summary to allocate local work through HMCGeometryScaledBudge
Its first attempt budget is

                            B0 = clamp (⌈cd d mgeom ⌉ , Bmin , Bmax,0 ) ,

where mgeom is a clipped multiplier built from condition, anisotropy, and regularization
pressure. Later attempts grow as

                                     Bk = min(Bmax , B0 2k ).

Bootstrap screens use a smaller square-root dimension rule,
                                         l √         m             
                         Nboot = clamp     c√d d mgeom , Nmin , Nmax ,

with a discarded initialization segment chosen as a fixed fraction of the screen length. This
preparation allocation does not establish sufficient posterior equilibration; the separate
assessment is described in Chapter 47.
    These formulas are heuristics, not posterior convergence criteria. They explain his-
torical stage budgets and the geometry-based preparation policies that remain available.
The current candidate-set search freezes its own measurement and verification allocations
and finite evidence_rungs. The convenience initial allocation comes from the accep-
tance policy’s minimum block evidence; target-specific adequacy must still be checked.
Geometry-derived preparation does not silently change that declared search allocation.


43.4         Timing And Progress
Wall-clock limits are treated differently from statistical tuning budgets. A stage may
run for a long time because the model is large but still making meaningful progress.
BayesFilter therefore separates:

       progress evidence, such as stage transitions, updated mass summaries, changed
        step-size hashes, changed trajectory hashes, repair decisions, and fresh verification
        summaries;

       emergency caps, which are machine-protection limits rather than claims that the
        sampler has failed scientifically.
43.5. FIXED-CENTER SCORE CURVATURE                                                       447

    Current candidate-set tuning records attempted calls, reserved mandatory work, a
conservative gradient-work estimate, and elapsed time including preparation. It checks
the declared wall limit at preparation progress boundaries and between bounded nu-
merical chunks; native calls require an external process limit for hard preemption. At-
tempted chunks are charged before execution, including a failed native call; completed
saved chunks are not charged again on resume. Unfundable peers remain pending while
affordable reserved work can proceed. The older staged timeout settings belong to his-
torical schedules. Neither kind of timeout is evidence against the posterior unless a
predeclared continuation veto says so; incomplete searches preserve their evidence and
remaining work.


43.5       Fixed-Center Score Curvature
Let c be an unchanged reviewed center and z a standardized local offset. Writing gz for
the score in those coordinates, BayesFilter fits
                          gz (c) − gz (c + z) ≈ Pz z,   Pz = Cz−1 .                   (43.1)
This relation identifies a local score derivative only when its fit and stability diagnostics
pass. It does not require gz (c) = 0, so it is not a Hessian-at-MAP statement. Score
magnitude is explanatory telemetry; curvature stability is the geometry target for this
API.
   The dense comparator estimates a symmetric Pz directly and preserves it before SPD
projection. The structured route parameterizes Cz and predicts with its inverse. Co-
variance parameters preserve SPD by construction, whereas the score equation consumes
precision.


43.6       One- and Two-Factor Covariance Geometry
For q ∈ {1, 2}, let D = diag(σ1 , . . . , σN ) and let row Li contain the factor loadings of
coordinate i. The covariance is
                               R = diag 1 − ∥Li ∥22 + LL⊤ ,         ∥Li ∥22 < 1.
                                                       
              Cz = DRD,                                                               (43.2)
The row-ball transform enforces strict interior loadings. For independent standard nor-
mals Fk and ei , the same correlation follows from
                               v
                    q          u       q                             q
                   X           u     X                               X
                                           2
             xi =      ρki Fk + 1 −
                               t          ρki ei ,  corr(xi , xj ) =   ρki ρkj . (43.3)
                   k=1                 k=1                            k=1

The implementation decodes unconstrained variables to Cz , obtains Pz by a Cholesky
solve inside every objective evaluation, and predicts Pz z. It returns both matrices so
callers cannot silently reverse them.
    One factor has N deviation coordinates and N loadings, hence 2N continuous pa-
rameters. The largest-absolute loading is constrained positive to remove the discrete sign
ambiguity. Two factors begin with N + 2N coordinates. A two-row triangular anchor
forces one loading to zero, leaving 3N − 1 continuous parameters; positive anchor di-
agonals remove discrete sign symmetries. A prediction-Jacobian rank check rejects an
unidentified second factor. Factor columns and rotations are nuisance representations:
covariance and precision are the downstream objects.
448                      CHAPTER 43. MASS MATRICES AND LOCAL GEOMETRY

43.7       Cloud Size, Reuse, and Escalation
The implemented search-count rule is
          (
            N 2,                        N ≤ 10,
  m(N ) =                                                     meven = 2 ⌈m(N )/2⌉ .     (43.4)
            100 + (N − 10) log(N − 10), N > 10,

It is a user-selected computational policy, not a sample-complexity theorem. The search
uses stateless randomized orthogonal frames and antithetic pairs. Finite nonzero earlier
rows within the current standardized radius may be reused for training only. Every struc-
tured replicate still supplies at least 4N fresh rows, split between training and selection
holdout. Fixed-center selection adds at least 2N fresh audit rows that are used only after
selection.
    Both APIs try one factor before two. The fixed-center route fits two factors only
when one-factor fit, holdout, or cross-replicate stability fails, or when the caller explicitly
requests a two-factor shrinkage target. The sequential proposal path follows the same
one-before-two order. Its trust-region quadratic proposes a step, but the exact target
value and score determine actual improvement and acceptance; regression never replaces
the posterior. The fixed-center path does not propose a new center.


43.8       Stability, Consensus, and Fallback
Every requested replicate retains raw eigenvalues and inertia. Pairwise diagnostics include
generalized-eigenvalue spread, trace-normalized Frobenius and operator differences, and
principal angles for a caller-declared dominant subspace. Projection burden and selection-
holdout error are separate gates. Omitted caps make these quantities descriptive and
prohibit HMC-canary eligibility; the DZ5 case does not define universal thresholds.
   For admissible SPD precision replicates Ks , convex consensus shrinkage is
                             S
                             X
                        −1
               K̄ = S              Ks ,   Kλ = (1 − λ)K̄ + λT,      0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.          (43.5)
                             s=1

This is plain convex shrinkage of designed score-regression fits, not the classical Ledoit–
Wolf estimator. No closed-form Ledoit–Wolf intensity is used. The caller supplies a finite
weight grid containing zero and one. Training and selection-holdout evidence select the
weight; a disjoint audit cloud can veto but cannot alter it.
   The fail-closed order is:
  (i) a stable, identified, holdout-passing one-factor precision;

 (ii) a stable, identified two-factor precision when one factor is inadequate;

(iii) a stable dense consensus combined with an explicitly selected, stable, identified
      structured target;

 (iv) if no structured target is supported, a stable dense consensus combined with its
      diagonal;

 (v) diagonal-only output as an explicitly reviewed diagnostic or operational artifact,
     never an automatic scientific promotion.
43.8. STABILITY, CONSENSUS, AND FALLBACK                                           449

An inadmissible raw dense family cannot be repaired by diagonalizing its projected con-
sensus. Identity is not an automatic fallback. If no branch passes, BayesFilter returns
geometry readiness blocked.
Chapter 44

Boundary Handling and Safe
Gradients

Boundary handling is part of the posterior target. Parameters can leave the station-
ary, positive-definite, or economically admissible region during HMC warmup. A robust
implementation must handle those proposals without crashing the chain or returning
non-finite gradients.


44.1       Finite Invalid Returns
The preferred policy is:

  (i) detect invalid regions before fragile factorizations where possible;

 (ii) return either the exact support-rejection value (−∞) or a declared finite fallback
      scalar for a modified target;

(iii) if a finite fallback scalar is used, return the exact derivative of that same scalar;

 (iv) record the invalid reason in diagnostics;

 (v) keep the behavior stable under JIT compilation.

    This policy is not a mathematical trick to make an invalid model valid. The exact
support-rejection contract and the finite modified-target contract are different mathe-
matical objects and must be named as such. A finite fallback may keep sampler control
flow in a compiled finite-valued regime, but it does not by itself guarantee rejection or
preserve the exact support-restricted target.


44.2       Boundary Checklist
Every HMC target should state its policy for prior support, parameter transforms, station-
arity or determinacy restrictions, covariance pivots, solve residuals, non-finite likelihoods,
and non-finite gradients.

                                             450
44.3. RANK, CHART, AND AFFINE-SUPPORT BOUNDARIES                                      451

44.3      Rank, Chart, and Affine-Support Boundaries
A singular Gaussian score is a smooth local object only on a fixed-rank, fixed-chart,
fixed-support stratum. Rank changes, pivot changes, QR sign changes, support changes,
and signed-weight PSD boundaries are not ordinary interior points of that score program.
BayesFilter therefore distinguishes:

    an on-support fixed branch, which returns the affine-support value and its analytical
     derivative;

    an off-support observation, which has exact value −∞ under the singular law and
     no admitted classical score; and

    a rank or chart crossing, which invalidates the frozen score branch and requires a
     new value-only preflight before another differentiated run.

The implementation reports these events instead of adding an undeclared nugget or dif-
ferentiating through SVD rank discovery. Consequently, the fixed-rank score is suitable
only for HMC targets whose trajectories remain inside a predeclared stratum or whose
outer target logic handles boundary rejection. This is a bounded differentiability claim,
not a claim of a globally smooth singular-covariance posterior.
Chapter 45

Occasionally Binding Constraints,
Gradient Discontinuities, and a
Failed Hypothesis

45.1      Purpose and scope
This chapter documents a research hypothesis that was mathematically wrong, the rigor-
ous audit that exposed it, and the lessons learned. It is preserved here not as a correct
method but as an instructive failure: an example of how plausible-sounding geometric
reasoning, when not grounded in explicit derivations, can lead to a research program built
on a false premise.
   The hypothesis was that a softplus-smoothed occasionally binding constraint, when
composed with an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) recursion inside an HMC target, cre-
ates gradient discontinuities that require specialized event-aware integration or neural
transport. An adversarial audit proved this claim false: the composed map is C ∞ wher-
ever the UKF covariance remains positive definite, so no gradient discontinuity exists.
The real difficulty—if any—is stiffness (high curvature), which belongs to the smooth
geometry and calls for step-size reduction or preconditioning, not for event detection.
   The chapter structure follows the scientific autopsy method:

  1. State the wrong hypothesis and its narrative motivation.

  2. Present the rigorous mathematical rebuttal, with full derivations.

  3. Identify the specific errors: where intuition diverged from proof, where claims lacked
     anchors, and where terminology conflated distinct geometric cases.

  4. Extract durable lessons for research discipline and claim verification.

    Reader responsibility. This chapter does not present a correct sampling method.
Its value is diagnostic: it shows what a wrong claim looks like when stated precisely, how
to audit one rigorously, and how to distinguish “seems like it should cause trouble” from
“proven to cause trouble.”

                                           452
45.2. THE FAILED HYPOTHESIS                                                               453

45.2         The failed hypothesis
45.2.1        Narrative form
In a shadow-rate term-structure model or New Keynesian model with an occasionally
binding zero lower bound, the forward yield curve or policy rate is bounded below by
some ℓ (typically 0 or a small negative effective lower bound). A hard censoring rule

                                          it = max{ℓ, i⋆t }                             (45.1)

is continuous but has a kinked gradient at i⋆t = ℓ. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo remains
valid for continuous kinked targets when the nondifferentiable set has Lebesgue measure
zero1 , but leapfrog integration may be inefficient near the kink.
    A natural smoothing strategy replaces the hard max with a softplus approximation:
                                                                          
                                        (u−ℓ)/a                        u−ℓ
                  s(u) = ℓ + a log(1 + e        ) = ℓ + a · softplus         ,   (45.2)
                                                                        a

where a > 0 is a scale parameter. As a → 0, s(u) → max{ℓ, u} pointwise. The softplus is
smooth: it is a composition of C ∞ functions (translation, scaling, exponential, logarithm),
so s ∈ C ∞ (R).
    The wrong hypothesis (retracted). In a nonlinear state-space model where the
observation map involves (45.2), if the marginal likelihood is computed via an Unscented
Kalman Filter, the composed parameter-to-log-likelihood map can exhibit gradient dis-
continuities when the latent shadow rate crosses the bound deeply. Specifically, when the
state drifts far below the bound, the UKF covariance collapses, sigma points cluster, and
the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to parameters jumps discontinuously. This
creates a “continuous-kink” geometry that ordinary HMC handles inefficiently and that
motivates event-aware integration or neural transport.
    This hypothesis was recorded in a survey manuscript (“Bayesian Inference for Non-
linear Models with a Genuine Zero Lower Bound,” §7, August 2026 draft) and motivated
an 11-week, 1000 GPU-hour research plan targeting event-aware HMC (Tran & Kleppe
reflection/refraction), UKF variance inflation, and neural surrogate training.

45.2.2        Why it seemed plausible
The hypothesis rested on several intuitively appealing but unverified steps:

  1. Softplus curvature. For small a, the second derivative s′′ (u) = O(a−1 ) grows
     large, suggesting stiffness.

  2. UKF sensitivity loss. When the latent rate is far below the bound, s′ (u) ≈ 0,
     so the observation Jacobian Ht ≈ 0 and the Kalman gain Kt ≈ 0. The filtered
     covariance Pt|t approaches the predicted Pt|t−1 , and the observation becomes unin-
     formative.

  3. Sigma-point clustering. As Pt → 0, unscented sigma points collapse toward the
     mean, and the UKF’s quadrature-based likelihood approximation changes charac-
     ter.
  1
      Afshar and Domke (2015), “Reflection, Refraction, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.”
454          CHAPTER 45. CONSTRAINTS AND GRADIENT DISCONTINUITIES

  4. Parameter sensitivity amplification. If Pt is small and parameter-sensitive,
     and if the innovation covariance St = Ht Pt Ht⊤ + R is also small, then ∥∇θ log p(yt |
     y1:t−1 , θ)∥ could amplify rapidly.
  5. Analogy to hard kinks. Since the softplus “approximates” the hard max, and
     hard max has a kinked gradient, perhaps the softplus inherits a “near-kink” that
     becomes a discontinuity under composition with the UKF recursion.
   None of these steps is individually absurd. Together, they painted a picture of a
smooth function that, when embedded in a recursive filter and differentiated with re-
spect to parameters, might develop jump discontinuities. The error was not checking the
conclusion with a derivation.


45.3      The rigorous rebuttal
An adversarial audit (Codex, September 2026) subjected the hypothesis to mandatory
derivations and fixed-verdict vocabulary. The audit proved the central mathematical
claim false. We reproduce the key results here.

45.3.1     Softplus smoothness and curvature bound
Proposition 45.1 (Softplus is C ∞ , not kinked). The softplus map (45.2) is infinitely
differentiable with bounded derivatives on compact sets. Its first and second derivatives
are
                                                       σ(z)(1 − σ(z))
                         s′ (u) = σ(z),      s′′ (u) =                ,            (45.3)
                                                             a
where z = (u − ℓ)/a and σ(z) = 1/(1 + e−z ) is the logistic function. The supremum of
the second derivative is
                                                       1
                                        sup s′′ (u) = .                            (45.4)
                                        u∈R           4a
Proof. Write s(u) = ℓ + a log(1 + ez ) where z = (u − ℓ)/a. The logarithm, exponential,
and affine maps are all C ∞ on their domains, and the composition is C ∞ on R.

45.3.2     UKF composition: no gradient jump
Proposition 45.2 (UKF composition remains smooth). Let θ ∈ Rp be parameters, and
let the UKF recursion compute a filtered mean mt (θ) and covariance Pt (θ) at each time
t, assuming Pt (θ) ≻ 0 for all θ in a neighborhood. Let the observation map be ht (xt , θ) =
s(g(xt , θ)), where s is the softplus (45.2) and g is smooth. If the UKF operations (Cholesky
factorization, matrix inversion, sigma-point propagation) are smooth in (mt , Pt , θ) on the
open cone Pt ≻ 0, then the log-likelihood ℓ(θ) = log p(y1:T | θ) computed via the UKF is
smooth in θ wherever all intermediate Pt (θ) remain positive definite.

Proof sketch. The UKF recursion is a finite composition of:

  1. Smooth parameter-dependent functions: mt (θ), Pt (θ), g(·, θ), s(·).

  2. Smooth matrix operations: addition, multiplication, Cholesky factorization LL⊤ =
     P (smooth on P ≻ 0), matrix inversion (smooth on invertible matrices).

  3. Smooth scalar operations: weighted sums (unscented mean), quadratic forms, log
     determinant log |S| (smooth when S ≻ 0).

45.3.3       The variance collapse mechanism is backwards
The survey manuscript claimed that when the latent shadow rate drifts far below the
bound (u ≪ ℓ), the UKF covariance collapses, amplifying parameter sensitivity and
creating gradient instability. The audit proved this mechanism backwards.

Proposition 45.3 (Variance preservation under insensitive observations). In the scalar
observation case, let m−     −                                                 −

Proof. As Ht → 0, the innovation covariance St = Ht Pt− Ht + R → R > 0. The Kalman

   The observation is uninformative about the shadow depth: it provides no information
to shrink the variance. The filtered variance equals the predicted variance, which can

   The survey’s §7.1 narrative inverted cause and effect. Insensitive observations preserve

45.3.4       Innovation covariance bound: no unbounded inverse
The survey claimed that variance collapse could make the innovation covariance St small,
causing its inverse St−1 to amplify parameter derivatives unboundedly. This is also false.

Proposition 45.4 (Innovation covariance lower bound). For St = Ht Pt− Ht⊤ + R with
R ≻ 0, we have St ⪰ R, hence ∥St−1 ∥ ≤ ∥R−1 ∥ in operator norm.

Proof. Since Ht Pt− Ht⊤ ⪰ 0 (positive semidefinite) and R ≻ 0 (positive definite), St =
Ht Pt− Ht⊤ + R ⪰ R. For positive definite matrices, A ⪰ B ≻ 0 implies A−1 ⪯ B −1 , so
St−1 ⪯ R−1 , giving ∥St−1 ∥ ≤ ∥R−1 ∥.

   Consequence. The measurement noise covariance R (fixed at 5×10−4 in the fixture)
bounds the innovation inverse from above, regardless of Pt collapse. The survey’s §7.2
amplification mechanism does not follow from variance collapse alone.

45.4      Specific errors in the failed hypothesis
We now catalog the precise points where the hypothesis diverged from mathematical
reality.

45.4.1     Error 1: Confusing stiffness with discontinuity
What was claimed: “The softplus creates gradient discontinuities when composed with
UKF filtering.”
   What is true: The softplus has curvature s′′ = O(1/a), which for small a is large
but finite and continuous. This is stiffness, a property of smooth geometry. Stiffness
makes small step sizes necessary for leapfrog stability; it does not create a discontinuity.
   Why the error persisted: The informal language “the gradient becomes very
sensitive” was interpreted as “the gradient jumps,” and the limiting behavior s(u) →
max{ℓ, u} as a → 0 was misread as implying that the finite-a softplus inherits the hard
max’s kink. Neither inference is valid without a proof.

45.4.2     Error 2: Inverting the variance collapse mechanism
What was claimed: “When the latent shadow rate drifts far below the bound, the
UKF covariance collapses, creating gradient amplification.”
    What is true: When s′ (u) → 0 (deep below bound), the observation Jacobian
Ht → 0, the Kalman gain Kt → 0, and the filtered covariance Pt|t → Pt− (preserved,
not collapsed). The observation is uninformative, so it neither shrinks nor amplifies the
variance.
    Why the error persisted: The narrative confused two different regimes: (i) infor-
mative observations near the kink, which can shrink variance and make the filter sen-
sitive, versus (ii) uninformative observations far below the bound, which leave variance
unchanged. The survey conflated these and concluded that deep-below-bound implies
collapse.

45.4.3     Error 3: Unbounded inverse claim without the S ⪰ R
           bound
What was claimed: “Variance collapse makes the innovation covariance St small, caus-
ing St−1 to amplify gradients unboundedly.”
   What is true: St = Ht Pt Ht⊤ + R ⪰ R > 0 always, so ∥St−1 ∥ ≤ ∥R−1 ∥ is bounded by
the measurement noise covariance, regardless of Pt .
45.4. SPECIFIC ERRORS IN THE FAILED HYPOTHESIS                                          459

   Why the error persisted: The derivation in the survey computed dS and d(log |S|)
but did not check the S ⪰ R lower bound before asserting amplification. The mechanism
was plausible-sounding but not derived.

45.4.4     Error 4: Misunderstanding the sigma-point limit
What was claimed: “As Pt → 0, sigma points undergo a simultaneous regime flip or
cluster jump that creates discontinuous parameter sensitivity.”
    What is true: As Pt → 0, all sigma points converge to the mean mt , and the
unscented mean ŷt → h(mt ) smoothly. The UKF becomes an extended Kalman filter in
this limit; there is no flip.
    Why the error persisted: The intuition that “collapsing sigma points must do
something discontinuous” was never tested with a Taylor expansion. The correct limit is
a smooth convergence, not a jump.

45.4.5     Error 5: Convention collision in scaling statements
The survey manuscript used the symbol α with two different meanings:
    In §7 (UKF discontinuities): α as temperature parameter, where the softplus is
     written s(u) = (1/α) log(1 + eα(u−ℓ) ), so α = 1/a in our notation.
    In §13 (model specification): α as the scale parameter itself, matching our a.
    These are reciprocals: αtemp = 1/αscale . Every statement of the form “curvature is
O(α)” is correct under one convention and wrong under the other. The survey’s O(α)
scaling claims are internally inconsistent, making it impossible to verify whether stiffness
grows or shrinks with the stated parameter.
    Why the error persisted: The two sections were written at different times, and
no global symbol audit caught the reuse. This is a cautionary example of how notation
drift can corrupt quantitative claims.

45.4.6     Error 6: Taxonomy confusion
The survey manuscript (§2) correctly defines four posterior geometries:
  1. Case 1: Continuous kinked target, it = max{ℓ, i⋆t }, ∆U = 0.
  2. Case 2: Deterministic branch jump, ∆U ̸= 0 from selection between equilibria.
  3. Case 3: Mixed discrete-continuous target (stochastic regime variable).
  4. Case 4: Multiplicity or nonexistence (no well-defined posterior until a selection rule
     is added).
   The survey’s §7 then claims the softplus UKF creates a Case 1 (kinked) or Case 3
(value jump) geometry, contradicting the §13 case-study text that explicitly classifies the
UKF route as smooth (no kink, no jump). This internal contradiction was not noticed
until the audit.
   Why the error persisted: Different sections were drafted with different claims
in mind, and no cross-section consistency check was performed before the hypothesis
hardened into a research plan.
460            CHAPTER 45. CONSTRAINTS AND GRADIENT DISCONTINUITIES

45.5         What the executed evidence actually shows
An 8-parameter joint HMC run (G2.3, filter-free, hard-max target mf c1 k40 hardmax)
was executed and passed a convergence gate at max R̂ = 1.0090 after warmup 8000 /
draws 8000. The bottleneck was parameter θ8 (log FX measurement noise scale) with
ESS 848.7, about 5× slower than the drift parameters.
    The G2.3 result document (September 2026) offers two candidate explanations for the
θ8 bottleneck:

  1. Funnel geometry: Log noise scales in a non-centered parameterization sit in a
     funnel against the latent innovations. The conditional curvature of the latent-to-
     parameter map varies with the noise scale itself, so a fixed dense mass matrix cannot
     flatten the geometry.

  2. Trajectory-length periodicity: In a stiff direction, leapfrog trajectories can re-
     turn near their starting point after an integer multiple of the period, producing
     high acceptance but poor exploration. This would explain the non-monotone mix-
     ing (L=64 worse than L=32 and L=128).

   Neither explanation invokes UKF filtering, gradient discontinuities, or softplus kinks,
because:

       The executed target used the hard max (C1), not softplus (S1).

       The executed target was filter-free joint HMC over latent states, not UKF-marginalized.

       No UKF implementation exists in the bayesfilter/hardbound/ package to test.

    The measured evidence does not support the UKF discontinuity hypothesis. It sup-
ports a different bottleneck (funnel or periodicity) in a different target (hard-max joint
HMC) that passed its convergence gate without requiring event-aware integration or neu-
ral transport.


45.6         The research plan that followed the wrong hy-
             pothesis
Based on the false discontinuity claim, an 11-week research plan was drafted with the
following phases:

  1. Phase 1 (weeks 1-2, 20 GPU-hours): Measurement. Build a UKF-filtered
     softplus target, run toy-model and G2.3 diagnostics, and measure gradient discon-
     tinuities at kink crossings.

  2. Phase 2 (weeks 3-4, 100 GPU-hours): Event-aware integration. Implement
     Tran & Kleppe (2025) reflection/refraction HMC (GRHMC) for the measured dis-
     continuities.

  3. Phase 3 (weeks 5-6, 80 GPU-hours): UKF variance inflation. Inflate UKF
     covariance to prevent collapse, retune HMC, and measure impact on mixing.
45.7. LESSONS FOR RESEARCH DISCIPLINE                                                461

  4. Phase 4 (weeks 7-10, 800 GPU-hours): Neural surrogate. Train a Hamiltonian
     Neural Network on the discontinuous UKF target and use it as an HMC proposal
     or warping.

  5. Phase 5 (week 11): Production candidate selection. Rank methods by ESS/gra-
     dient ¿ 0.1 threshold and promote to production.

   Total budget: 1000 GPU-hours over 11 weeks.

45.6.1     Why the plan was abandoned
The adversarial audit (M1-M25, September 2026) delivered 17 “wrong relative to stated
target” verdicts, 6 “unsupported” verdicts, 1 “correct,” and 1 “heuristic only.” The
five mandatory mathematical derivations (M1, M3, M4, M5, M6) all contradicted the
hypothesis. Specifically:

    M1: Softplus is C ∞ ; gradient jump claim is false.

    M4: Variance collapse mechanism is backwards.

    M5: Innovation covariance bound prevents unbounded amplification.

    M6: Sigma-point limit is smooth convergence, not a flip.

    M15: Plan contradicts master program’s binding non-goals (filter-free, no event-
     aware HMC).

    M16: G2.3 evidence uses hard-max joint HMC, not UKF-filtered softplus.

    M20: Surrogate-target HMC is biased, not exact.

    The plan was retracted in full, the survey §7 scheduled for removal, and the research
direction closed. No phase was executed.


45.7      Lessons for research discipline
This failure offers several durable lessons for structuring research claims and avoiding
similar errors.

45.7.1     Lesson 1: Derive, don’t narrate
The failure mode. The hypothesis was built from a chain of plausible-sounding steps:
“softplus is steep” → “UKF becomes sensitive” → “gradients jump.” Each local step
seemed reasonable, but the composition was never verified with an end-to-end derivation.
   The corrective discipline. For any mathematical claim that motivates expensive
work (measurement, tuning, training, 1000 GPU-hours):

  1. Write the claim as a proposition with explicit hypotheses and conclusion.

  2. Derive the conclusion from the hypotheses, or cite a theorem that does so.

  3. If the derivation is “obvious,” write it anyway—errors hide in the obvious.
462            CHAPTER 45. CONSTRAINTS AND GRADIENT DISCONTINUITIES

  4. If the derivation is blocked by missing definitions or assumptions, treat that as a
     signal that the claim is not yet ready.

   Narrative momentum (“it makes sense that X would cause Y ”) is not evidence. A
correct derivation or a measurement artifact is evidence.

45.7.2       Lesson 2: Distinguish stiffness from discontinuity
The failure mode. The softplus second derivative s′′ = O(1/a) grows large as a → 0,
and the pointwise limit lima→0 s(u) = max{ℓ, u} is kinked. These facts were conflated
into “the softplus is almost kinked, so it acts like a kink.”
    The corrective discipline. Stiffness (large but finite and continuous derivatives)
and discontinuity (actual jumps) are distinct geometric classes with distinct samplers:
                                                       −1/2
       Stiffness calls for step-size reduction (ϵ = O(λmax )), mass-matrix preconditioning,
        Riemannian metrics, or trust-region methods. Leapfrog remains valid; it is merely
        expensive.

       Discontinuity calls for event detection, reflection/refraction, or discontinuous
        HMC variants that explicitly handle the jump in potential or gradient.

   A function that is C k for finite k ≥ 1 is not discontinuous. Treating smooth high-
curvature functions as discontinuous is a category error that leads to the wrong sampler.

45.7.3       Lesson 3: Check mechanisms in both directions
The failure mode. The narrative was “s′ → 0 causes variance collapse.” The Kalman
equations say s′ → 0 =⇒ Kt → 0 =⇒ Pt|t → Pt− (variance preserved). The correct
implication is the opposite of the claimed one, but the error was not caught because the
mechanism was stated in words, not equations.
   The corrective discipline. For any claimed causal mechanism A =⇒ B:

  1. Write the explicit equations or inequalities connecting A and B.

  2. Derive B from A using those equations.

  3. Derive the contrapositive: ¬B =⇒ ¬A. If the contrapositive is false, the original
     claim is false.

  4. Check whether B =⇒ A is also true, false, or independent. If “thus” appears in
     the narrative, verify that the implication actually points in the stated direction.

   Equations are bidirectional; they can be solved for any variable. A verbal “thus” can
point in the wrong direction without triggering an error signal.

45.7.4       Lesson 4: Anchor claims to code, not to plans
The failure mode. The hypothesis referenced “the UKF route” as if it existed. The sur-
vey described a UKF implementation (§13), and the research plan budgeted GPU-hours
for UKF experiments. Neither the description nor the plan constituted an implemen-
tation. The actual ‘bayesfilter/hardbound/‘ package contained no UKF recursion, no
45.7. LESSONS FOR RESEARCH DISCIPLINE                                                 463

‘tf.where‘ branching on parameter-dependent conditions, and no Cholesky factorization
inside an observation loop—none of the elements required for a UKF-marginalized target.
    The corrective discipline. Before claiming that “method X exhibits property Y ”:

  1. Locate the implementation of method X: file path, function name, call chain from
     entry point to the relevant operation.

  2. Run a minimal test that exercises the claimed property Y .

  3. Record the artifact (test output, diagnostic value, plot) as evidence.

   A plan to implement X is not an implementation of X. A survey section describing
X is not an implementation of X. An implementation is code that compiles and runs. If
the claim is about code that does not yet exist, state that explicitly: “If we implement
X, we conjecture Y .”

45.7.5     Lesson 5: Adversarial review catches what friendly re-
           view misses
The failure mode. The hypothesis was developed incrementally: a survey section here,
a research plan there, informal discussions, and gradual narrative convergence. Each local
decision seemed reasonable, and no single-author review caught the composition error.
    The corrective discipline. For research directions that commit significant resources
(time, compute, opportunity cost of alternative directions):

  1. Write a single self-contained document stating the hypothesis, the evidence for it,
     the research plan, and the expected outcome.

  2. Subject that document to adversarial review: a reviewer whose task is to find flaws,
     not to approve the plan.

  3. Require the reviewer to deliver mandatory derivations for key mathematical claims,
     not just a thumbs-up/thumbs-down verdict.

  4. Use fixed verdict vocabulary (correct, wrong relative to stated target, unsupported,
     not checked) to prevent evasive language (“reasonable,” “approximately,” “in some
     sense”).

  5. Treat “unsupported” the same as “wrong” for go/no-go decisions: if the evidence
     is missing, the claim is not ready.

   Friendly review surfaces misunderstandings and unclear exposition. Adversarial re-
view surfaces wrong claims that sound right. Both are necessary, but they are not the
same service.

45.7.6     Lesson 6: “Not checked” is not “probably fine”
The failure mode. Several sub-claims in the hypothesis were never verified: the UKF
implementation did not exist, the Tran & Kleppe (2025) paper was a dangling citation
(not in the bibliography, no full text available), the 800 GPU-hour Phase 4 budget had
no cost model, and the ESS/gradient ¿ 0.1 promotion threshold had no calibration to the
464             CHAPTER 45. CONSTRAINTS AND GRADIENT DISCONTINUITIES

measured ladder. Each of these was noted as “to be done later,” but the research plan
proceeded as if they were already validated.
   The corrective discipline. Distinguish three evidence states:

       Verified: A derivation, measurement, or cited theorem explicitly supports the
        claim.

       Unsupported: No evidence has been checked, but the claim might be true.

       Wrong: A derivation or measurement explicitly contradicts the claim.

    For go/no-go decisions, treat “unsupported” as a block, not as “probably fine.” A
hypothesis with three verified steps and two unsupported steps is not 60% validated; it
is unvalidated. The unsupported steps are gaps, not rounding errors.


45.8         What remains correct
Not every statement in the original hypothesis was wrong. We record the surviving claims
to avoid overcorrecting.

45.8.1        Stiffness is real
The softplus second derivative bound sup s′′ = 1/(4a) √ is correct. For small a, the cur-
vature is large, and the leapfrog stability bound ϵ < 2/ λmax can force small step sizes.
This is a genuine implementation challenge for HMC, even though it is not a discontinuity.
   What works for stiffness:

       Step-size adaptation (dual averaging with a conservative target acceptance rate).

       Dense or Riemannian mass-matrix adaptation to precondition the geometry.

       Trust-region or implicit integrators for severely stiff problems.

45.8.2        Hard kinks are different
The hard max it = max{ℓ, i⋆t } has a derivative that jumps from 0 to 1 at the boundary;
the derivative is undefined at equality. This can produce a continuous potential with a
discontinuous gradient. The validity of a Metropolis-corrected leapfrog proposal rests on
its reversible, volume-preserving composition of momentum kicks and position drifts, with
a fixed deterministic force convention and the exact endpoint energy. The measure-zero
boundary alone does not establish accurate integration or efficient exploration.
     Boundary methods must match the type of boundary. Pakman and Paninski [2014,
Section 2] solve the quadratic Hamiltonian exactly between reflections at truncation con-
straints. Their Bayesian Lasso extension (Section 4, equations 4.12–4.22) instead crosses
a continuous kink with continuous position and velocity, updating the region’s quadratic
dynamics. That special construction does not supply an integrator for an arbitrary
hard-max state-space posterior. Afshar and Domke [2015, Algorithm 1 and Section 5]
incorporate reflection or refraction at a jump ∆U in potential energy, with their volume-
preservation proof covering affine partition boundaries. When a crossing has ∆U = 0
and nonzero normal momentum, their refraction rule leaves that momentum unchanged.
45.8. WHAT REMAINS CORRECT                                                               465

Thus this rule alone does not correct the integration error caused by a continuous gradient
kink.
   Key distinction: The hard max is a Case 1 geometry (continuous kink, ∆U = 0).
The softplus is smooth (no kink, ∆U = 0, but large curvature). They are not the same,
and methods for one do not automatically apply to the other.


45.8.3     Filter choice matters for HMC targets
For nonlinear state-space models, the choice of filter (particle filter, extended Kalman fil-
ter, unscented Kalman filter, ensemble Kalman filter) determines the marginal likelihood
approximation and its gradient. Different filters have different:

    Bias-variance tradeoffs (bootstrap particle filter is unbiased but high-variance; UKF
     is deterministic but biased for highly nonlinear models).

    Differentiability (ordinary resampling is discontinuous; optimal-transport resam-
     pling is smooth but adds regularization).

    Computational cost (particle filter scales with particle count N ; UKF scales with
     state dimension d).

  The hypothesis was wrong about where the discontinuity arises (not in the softplus-
UKF composition), but correct that filter geometry matters for HMC.


45.8.4     Funnel geometry is a real bottleneck
The G2.3 leapfrog ladder result identified θ8 (log FX noise scale) as the bottleneck, with
ESS 848.7 vs 4000-5100 for drift parameters. The candidate explanation is funnel geom-
etry: in a non-centered parameterization, the conditional curvature of latent innovations
varies with the noise scale, creating a funnel that dense mass matrices cannot flatten.
    This is a real geometric challenge, independent of the failed UKF discontinuity hy-
pothesis. Standard repairs for funnel geometry include:

    Non-centered vs centered parameterization (already used in the executed G2.3 tar-
     get).

    QR reparameterization of the latent-to-observable Jacobian to decorrelate scales
     from rotations.

    Hierarchical priors on log scales to regularize extreme values.

    Partial centering chosen before sampling. Variationally inferred parameterization
     learns the interpolation between centered and non-centered coordinates during vari-
     ational preprocessing, then fixes it for HMC [Gorinova et al., 2020, Section 5.2 and
     Appendix C]. The variational objective does not guarantee that all posterior modes
     are represented.

   The funnel is a smooth geometry problem, not a discontinuity problem. It is orthog-
onal to the retracted UKF hypothesis.

45.9.1       This chapter in the BayesFilter monograph
This chapter is an autopsy, not a method. It documents a hypothesis that failed adver-
sarial review and was retracted. Its purpose is pedagogical: to show what a wrong claim
looks like when stated precisely, how to audit it rigorously, and how to avoid similar
errors.
    Readers implementing HMC for occasionally binding constraints should read:

       Chapter 44: Boundary handling and safe gradients (correct general treatment).

       Chapter 41: HMC for state-space models (correct filter-HMC integration).

       Pakman and Paninski [2014] for truncated Gaussian and piecewise-quadratic dy-
        namics, and Afshar and Domke [2015] for potential jumps across affine boundaries,
        with the distinctions above for a continuous kink.

       This chapter only for the cautionary example.


45.9.2       Relation to the retracted survey section
The failed hypothesis originated in §7 of the survey manuscript “Bayesian Inference for
Nonlinear Models with a Genuine Zero Lower Bound” (August 2026 draft). That section
is scheduled for retraction, and the survey will note:

        “An earlier draft (August 2026) included §7, which claimed that softplus-
        smoothed occasionally binding constraints create gradient discontinuities when
        composed with UKF filtering. This section was retracted in September 2026
        after an adversarial audit proved the central mathematical claim false. The
        softplus-UKF composition is C ∞ wherever the covariance remains positive
        definite; the claimed discontinuity does not exist. See BayesFilter monograph
        Chapter 45 for the full autopsy.”

  The survey’s correct Case 1-4 taxonomy (§2), particle-filter treatment (§6, §9-12), and
New Keynesian multiplicity analysis (§8) are unaffected and remain in the final version.


45.9.3       Relation to the abandoned research plan
The research plan “UKF Discontinuous-Gradient HMC Program” (August 26, 2026) was
archived without execution. Its five phases (measurement, event-aware integration, UKF
variance inflation, neural surrogate, production selection) were all predicated on the false
discontinuity hypothesis. The plan is preserved in the repository at

  docs/plans/ukf-discontinuous-gradient-hmc-research-plan-2026-08-26.md

with a header stating “RETRACTED: This plan was based on a mathematically false
hypothesis. See the Codex audit reply for the rebuttal.”
45.10. FINAL SUMMARY                                                                  467

45.9.4     Relation to executed work
The “Hard-Bound Kink-Target HMC Master Program” (Program A, August-September
2026) executed filter-free joint HMC on the hard-max target mf c1 k40 hardmax and
passed the G2.3 convergence gate. This work is unaffected by the failed UKF hypothesis,
because:

    Program A used the hard max (C1), not softplus (S1).

    Program A was filter-free (joint HMC over latent states), not UKF-marginalized.

    Program A’s binding non-goals explicitly excluded particle filters, UKF marginal
     likelihood, and event-aware HMC.

   The executed work stands as correct. The abandoned plan was a separate, unexecuted
proposal.


45.10       Final summary
The hypothesis: Softplus-smoothed occasionally binding constraints, when composed
with UKF filtering inside an HMC target, create gradient discontinuities that require
event-aware integration or neural transport.
    The verdict: Wrong relative to the stated target. The softplus is C ∞ , UKF
composition with smooth maps is smooth, and no gradient discontinuity exists. The
real difficulty—if any—is stiffness (high curvature O(1/a)), which is a smooth geometry
problem.
    The specific errors:

  1. Confusing stiffness with discontinuity.

  2. Inverting the variance collapse mechanism (s′ → 0 preserves variance, does not
     collapse it).

  3. Ignoring the S ⪰ R bound (innovation inverse is bounded by measurement noise).

  4. Misunderstanding the sigma-point limit (smooth convergence to linearization, not
     a flip).

  5. Convention collision (α used as both 1/a and a, inverting all scaling claims).

  6. Taxonomy confusion (softplus UKF is smooth, not Case 1 kinked or Case 3 value-
     jump).

   The lessons:

  1. Derive, don’t narrate.

  2. Distinguish stiffness from discontinuity.

  3. Check mechanisms in both directions.

  4. Anchor claims to code, not to plans.
468         CHAPTER 45. CONSTRAINTS AND GRADIENT DISCONTINUITIES

  5. Adversarial review catches what friendly review misses.

  6. “Not checked” is not “probably fine.”

    The corrective action: Survey §7 retracted, research plan archived, hypothesis
closed. No phases executed, no GPU-hours spent. The failure was caught by adversarial
audit before resources were committed.
    The durable value: A worked example of how to structure, audit, and reject a
wrong hypothesis—and how to extract lessons that prevent the next one.
Chapter 46

XLA and JIT Compilation

BayesFilter uses JIT compilation as a production tool, not as a correctness argument. A
sampler is not fully compiled merely because an outer function is wrapped in tf.function.
The complete value-and-gradient path must be inside the compiled region, with static
shapes and compatible device placement.


46.1      Full-Pipeline Requirement
For HMC, the compiled path includes:

    parameter transform;

    model-provider maps;

    filtering likelihood;

    custom or autodiff gradient path;

    invalid-region branch;

    leapfrog transition or equivalent integrator.

If any component falls back to Python, retraces dynamically, or executes an opaque
noncompiled kernel, the implementation should be described as partially compiled.


46.2      Device and Shape Constraints
The DSGE XLA source notes emphasize two lessons that carry over to BayesFilter.
First, XLA compiles a function for a target platform, so mixing CPU-only custom calls
with GPU-targeted operations inside one JIT block can fail. Second, XLA requires
static shapes. Dynamic metadata should be encoded as values or opaque compile-time
metadata, not as changing tensor ranks.
    The practical policy is phase separation: solve or model-construction phases may be
compiled separately from the filtering/HMC phase if they have different device require-
ments. A monolithic JIT block is valuable only when it actually contains compatible
operations.

                                           469
470                                   CHAPTER 46. XLA AND JIT COMPILATION

46.3      Explicit CPU Multiprocess Cloud Evaluation
Independent fixed-center score rows may be evaluated through CPUXLACloudEvaluator.
This is an explicitly selected CPU route, not an automatic fallback after a GPU failure.
The evaluator creates a persistent spawn-based process pool on its first cloud, after the
row count is known, and reuses that pool for later calls. Pool creation temporarily
supplies the CPU-only environment inherited before spawn can re-import the caller’s main
module, and then restores the parent environment. A lightweight bootstrap module that
has no framework imports fails closed unless it entered with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=
-1 and memory growth enabled. It records any framework modules already imported
under that inherited environment, then compiles and warms one static B = 1 value-and-
score function with XLA for reuse. Results are restored to input order, child exceptions
propagate, and each child returns its bootstrap provenance.
   The user-directed worker baseline is

                                 W = max(1, ⌊C/3⌋) ,

clamped to the first cloud’s task count. Here C is the physical-core count from psutil.
cpu_count(logical=False) when available; otherwise the logical os.cpu_count() fall-
back and its provenance are recorded. Callers may override W . This policy is not a
performance optimum.
   Each completed row advances completed rows. A heartbeat emitted while waiting
has semantic progress=false and is not completed work. Time budgets remain safety
guards rather than mandatory kill times for a process that continues to publish semantic
progress.
   The child-process XLA smoke proves only that the tested spawn, import, compile,
and evaluation route executes. It does not establish scaling or CPU/GPU superiority.
Target-only XLA parity remains separate from full-chain HMC XLA. GPU execution has
an independent allocator contract: TF_FORCE_GPU_ALLOW_GROWTH=true before import
and verified memory growth on every visible GPU. These CPU tests do not establish
GPU readiness.
Chapter 47

Diagnostics and Failure Taxonomy

Diagnostics are evidence about failures and geometry. They are not proofs of conver-
gence. BayesFilter should report diagnostics at three levels: filter evaluation, derivative
evaluation, and sampler behavior.


47.1       Filter and Derivative Diagnostics
Filter diagnostics include factor pivots, reconstruction errors, solve residuals, condition
numbers, invalid-region counts, and finite-value checks. Derivative diagnostics include
score/Hessian finite checks, symmetry errors, backend parity deltas, finite-difference resid-
uals, and custom-gradient parity. For SVD or eigendecomposition paths, singular-value
or eigenvalue gap telemetry is mandatory before HMC claims are made.


47.2       Sampler Diagnostics
Sampler diagnostics include acceptance rate, divergences, energy behavior, effective sam-
ple size, split R-hat, mass-matrix conditioning, and tree depth if NUTS is used diagnos-
tically. Short clean runs are smoke tests. They can justify the next experiment, but they
do not establish convergence for an industrial target.


47.3       Warm-up and posterior precision
A tuning allocation answers how much computation to spend learning geometry and
qualifying a frozen transition. It does not answer how long the resulting chain must run
to forget its initialization. BayesFilter therefore keeps all verified (L, ϵ) pairs and asks
the caller to choose a member before posterior assessment. No R-hat, ESS or MCSE
threshold changes tuning membership.
    The selected member runs a separate discarded warm-up, followed by cumulative
retained draws. The shared keyword configuration inherits a minimum of 2,000 warm-up
transitions per chain, a recent window of 1,000, modern R-hat at most 1.05, and a cap
of 10,000. These numbers are operational owner-policy choices; they are not estimates
of a sufficient burn-in for every target. Stan’s windowed adaptation likewise allocates
configured warm-up to fast step-size and slow metric updates. Finishing that schedule is
not a proof of stationarity.

                                            471
472                     CHAPTER 47. DIAGNOSTICS AND FAILURE TAXONOMY

    HMCPosteriorAssessmentPolicy makes the additional requirements explicit: mini-
mum bulk and tail ESS during warm-up and retention, the number of consecutive suc-
cessful warm-up checks, and accuracy targets for the retained estimators. Every eligible
look reports rank-normalized split and folded R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, original-scale mean
ESS and mean MCSE. Bulk and tail ESS use the Stan/ArviZ initial-positive, initial-
monotone recursion, with an explicit method identifier in the assessment report. The
separate precision-policy autocorrelation estimator retains the TFP convention described
below. Custom callbacks add requirements; they cannot replace core health and R-hat
checks. The archived wrapper retains its historical strict inequality and declared coordi-
nate/ESS screens, while using the same diagnostic arithmetic. The generic entry point
for a verified member is run_hmc_posterior.
    Repeated successful windows are useful evidence of stability in the region visited.
Overlapping windows are not independent replications, and all chains can remain in one
unrepresentative mode. A small R-hat cannot detect a mode no chain visits. Model-
specific functionals, event indicators and log density can be monitored with a named
quantities_fn and a stable quantities_id. If the warm-up cap is exhausted, the
result reports inconclusive equilibration and does not start retained inference. Warm-up
draws remain archived and are always excluded from posterior estimates.
    A short recent window can itself contain too little effective information for the readi-
ness screen, even after initialization bias has decayed. Increasing the warm-up cap while
keeping that window fixed does not increase the information available at each check. A
target-specific study should therefore declare both its recent-window length and its total
allowance, using pilot dependence estimates to plan them and fresh replications to assess
delivery. Changing these settings defines a new posterior policy and checkpoint; it does
not revoke or retune the verified kernel.
    The shared configuration also permits an explicitly justified finite budget exception:
max_results_per_chain sets the bound and count_budget_reason records why a bound
above 10000 is needed. Warm-up and retained maxima must lie within it. The serialized
posterior policy labels the nondefault allocation; the canonical 10000 default and all
health, R-hat and precision requirements are unchanged.

At ρ = 0.995, four unit-variance chains therefore need about 39900 retained draws each to
attain mean MCSE 0.05 in this planning approximation. A cap of 10000 is inadequate for
that typical precision requirement even when the transition and uncertainty calculation
are correct. The actual stopping rule also depends on noisy diagnostic estimates and
requires its own calibration; this count is neither a burn-in estimate nor a universal lower
bound for HMC.
    The autocorrelation option retains the identified TFP 0.25 positive-pairs ESS calcu-
lation. Rank-normalized bulk ESS is useful for exploration diagnostics, but original-scale
mean uncertainty needs the ESS of the actual functional. For a quantile, BayesFilter
follows the indicator-ESS and order-statistic construction in Vehtari et al. [2021, section
4.4], with the explicitly named TFP positive-pairs indicator ESS. The pooled percentile
preserves equal interpolation endpoints exactly: otherwise rounding a cutoff below a re-
peated value can change every indicator at that value and hence its estimated ESS. The
corrected quantile method has a versioned identifier in both the report and precision
policy, so a checkpoint from the earlier arithmetic cannot be silently reused. A constant
rare-event indicator or a tied zero-width quantile interval supplies no reliable accuracy
evidence.
474                      CHAPTER 47. DIAGNOSTICS AND FAILURE TAXONOMY

    The reported quantile MCSE approximates a standard error using central order statis-
tics. Multiplying it by 1.96 gives a symmetric diagnostic interval; this is not the same
finite-sample calculation as propagating the .025 and .975 probabilities directly to em-
pirical order statistics. Independent formula agreement checks the arithmetic, not the
coverage of either interval under actual HMC stopping. Finite diagnostics do not establish
the moments or mixing assumptions needed by any of these estimators.
    Each HMCPrecisionTarget specifies a mean or a quantile and an absolute MCSE tol-
erance, an MCSE-to-posterior-SD tolerance, or both. Accuracy is assessed on cumulative
retained draws. No supplied tolerance means precision_not_requested; a successful
diagnostic screen then carries no claim of sufficient estimator accuracy. At the retained
cap, unmet targets remain insufficient. Repeated MCSE screening is an operational stop-
ping rule: the implementation does not claim finite-sample or anytime-valid confidence
coverage. The asymptotic fixed-width results in Flegal and Gong [2013, sections 2–3.1 and
Appendix A] require additional regularity and estimator-consistency conditions. Lugsail
estimates uncertainty in retained means; it does not estimate how many burn-in draws
are enough. Experiments that compare stopping policies must declare the batch size,
minimum batch count and lugsail coefficients together with the recent-window length,
effective-sample-size requirements and persistence of readiness checks. The fixed-count
comparison uses the same declared estimator. A change to any of these choices requires
a fresh fit identity, including when a previous fit has already saved its final summary.
Otherwise a cached result could silently be attributed to a policy that never produced it.
    Absolute accuracy requirements must be interpreted in the units of the functional. For
independent normal
               √       observations with standard deviation s and total count N , the mean
has MCSE s/ N . The usual quantile approximation gives√       variance p(1 − p)/(N f (qp )2 );
substituting
p         √ p = 1/2 and normal density f (q1/2 ) = 1/( 2πs) yields median MCSE
   π/2 s/ N . Thus a broad normal coordinate can need more draws to estimate its
median than its mean at the same absolute tolerance. These independent-draw calcu-
lations help plan cost; correlated HMC can have different variances, including smaller
ones under negative dependence. A retained cap therefore requires inspecting quantity-
specific uncertainty and trajectory behavior before diagnosing a tuning failure. An unmet
accuracy requirement remains unmet even when R-hat is favorable.
    The diagnostic version bayesfilter.hmc_diagnostic_math.v2 corrects two prior
arithmetic errors: normal-score ranks use S + 1/4 in the denominator, and modern R-
hat is the square root of the variance ratio. Earlier reported threshold results require
recomputation from draws before current use. Adjacent-epoch drift statistics remain de-
scriptive: the old normalization omits covariance between adjacent epoch means and is
not a calibrated test. The legacy Phase 29 warmup screen still compares these statis-
tics with its configured heuristic thresholds. Those comparisons can reject that legacy
screen; they are not part of the common posterior assessment and do not have calibrated
significance levels.

      # descriptive acceptance or ESS differences do not establish a ranking.

    result[’wall_seconds’] = time.monotonic()-started
    (args.output_dir/’result.json’).write_text(json.dumps(result,indent=2,allow_nan=
    False)+’\n’)
    print(json.dumps({k:result[k] for k in (’passed’,’equilibration_status’,’
    precision_status’,’wall_seconds’)}))


if __name__ == ’__main__’:
    main()
47.4. FAILURE TAXONOMY                                                                  477

47.4      Failure Taxonomy
Common failure classes are:

    target-domain failures;

    factorization or solve failures;

    non-finite value or gradient failures;

    spectral derivative instability;

    JIT retracing or partial compilation;

    sampler geometry failures;

    unsupported missing-data or mask patterns.

Each failure should point to a next action: fix the model contract, change the backend,
add jitter or regularization, strengthen derivative validation, or downgrade the backend
to diagnostic use.


47.5      Curvature Diagnostic Roles
Fixed-center curvature diagnostics have explicit roles:

required gate finite raw matrices, caller-declared raw inertia, selection-holdout error,
     projection burden, complete pairwise stability caps, and the independent audit
     error;

promotion veto a failed required gate blocks nomination for an exact HMC mechanics
    canary;

repair trigger failed one-factor holdout can trigger an identified two-factor fit, while
     unstable dense curvature triggers structured or consensus analysis;

explanatory center score magnitude, optimizer iterations, descriptive runtimes, and any
     stability metric for which no cap was supplied.

    SPD projection does not convert failed raw curvature into a pass. Raw inertia and
matrices remain visible. Likewise, a low score is not a curvature gate and a stable nonzero-
score center is not a MAP. A locally useful geometry for an exact Metropolis-corrected
HMC canary remains unproved as a posterior covariance or global-mode Hessian.
    geometry readiness blocked rejects the current evidence and mass handoff. It does
not imply that the model, target, or curvature-preconditioning research direction has
failed.
Chapter 48

Transport Maps and Surrogate
Geometry

Transport maps and surrogates are downstream geometry tools. They can make an HMC
target easier to explore, but they cannot repair an invalid likelihood, an inconsistent
custom gradient, or a non-finite filter boundary. This chapter therefore depends on the
target, derivative, and diagnostics contracts already defined in the earlier chapters.


48.1       Transported Targets
Let q ∈ Rd denote the original unconstrained parameter and let

                                         q = Tψ (z)

be an invertible differentiable map from transported coordinates z to the original coor-
dinates. If the original target density is

                                   πQ (q) ∝ exp[−UQ (q)],

then the transported target is

                          UZ (z) = UQ (Tψ (z)) − log det JTψ (z) .                     (48.1)

Running HMC in z-space is target-preserving only when the sampler evaluates (48.1) and
its gradient. The Jacobian term is not optional. A learned map that is imperfect can still
be useful as a preconditioner, but omitting the change-of-variables correction changes the
target.


48.2       NeuTra Position
The Phase 2B literature gate accepted NeuTra only as transport and geometry support.
That is exactly the right status for BayesFilter. A NeuTra-like map can improve posterior
geometry by making the transformed target closer to a simple reference distribution. It
is not a correctness guarantee, and it is not a substitute for a valid filtering likelihood or
a derivative provider that matches the Metropolis value.
    The strategic use is:

                                             478
48.3. SURROGATE TARGETS                                                                 479

  (i) certify the filtering target and gradient first;

 (ii) train or choose a transport map to improve geometry;

(iii) run HMC on the Jacobian-corrected transported target;

(iv) compare diagnostics and effective sample size per unit time to the untransported
     or affine baseline.

If the map has poor tail behavior, bad inverse stability, or large Jacobian curvature, it
can make sampling worse even when it improves a training loss.


48.3       Surrogate Targets
A surrogate likelihood or surrogate Hamiltonian is a different object from a transport
map. If the surrogate changes the scalar log target used in the Metropolis correction,
the Markov chain targets the surrogate posterior unless a correction mechanism is added.
BayesFilter should record one of three statuses for every surrogate:

diagnostic surrogate used only for exploration, initialization, or comparison; no pos-
     terior correctness claim is made;

corrected surrogate used inside a delayed-acceptance or Metropolis-corrected scheme
     that evaluates the intended target before a sample is accepted;

target-defining surrogate deliberately defines the approximate posterior being sam-
     pled, with approximation error documented separately.

This distinction prevents a common failure mode: using a fast approximate filter or neural
surrogate for gradients and then interpreting the resulting chain as if it sampled the exact
filtering posterior.


48.4       Diagnostics
Transport diagnostics should be tied to sampler performance and target integrity:

    transformed-target finite value and finite gradient checks;

    log-Jacobian finite checks and inverse/forward reconstruction residuals;

    tail probes for large ∥z∥;

    acceptance rate, divergences, E-BFMI, and effective sample size per second relative
     to an affine baseline;

    shell-level Hessian or force diagnostics where available.

These diagnostics explain why a map helps or fails. They do not override a failed target
contract.
480          CHAPTER 48. TRANSPORT MAPS AND SURROGATE GEOMETRY

48.5      BayesFilter Policy
Transport and surrogate methods should enter BayesFilter after the exact or controlled
approximate likelihood path has been validated. They are valuable for large models be-
cause geometry can dominate HMC cost, but they sit on top of the filter contract rather
than underneath it. In particular, they should not be proposed as a fix for SVD spectral-
gradient instability, missing derivative guards, or partial XLA compilation. Those prob-
lems must be solved at the filter and sampler-contract layer first.
Chapter 49

Neural Transport Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo

This chapter gives a self-contained account of neural-transport Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
(NeuTra HMC) and documents the BayesFilter implementation and experiments available
in July 2026, followed by a September 2026 investigation of weak nonlinear learning in
the q20 target. The construction was introduced by Hoffman et al. [2019]; the derivation
and implementation below do not require the reader to consult that paper. The HMC
and transport mathematics, diagnostics, and five common truth-tail targets are derived
explicitly. Eight additional historical configurations are reported under their preserved
protocols. Four of those are inherited DSGE targets whose complete economic model
systems belong to their dedicated chapters and repositories; they are identified here at
the resolution needed to interpret the NeuTra evidence, but are not presented as self-
contained re-derivations of those economic models.


49.1      Motivation: geometry is often the HMC bot-
          tleneck
Let ϑ denote scientifically meaningful parameters and let y denote the observations.
Bayesian computation targets

                                             p(y | ϑ)p(ϑ)
                                p(ϑ | y) =                .                        (49.1)
                                                 p(y)

The evidence p(y) is normally unavailable, but HMC needs only an unnormalized log
posterior and its gradient. Constraints are first removed by a model chart ϑ = C(θ),
θ ∈ Rd . Thus the source-coordinate target used by computation is

                        eΘ (θ) = p(y | C(θ))p(C(θ)) |det JC (θ)| ,
                        π                                                          (49.2)
                        ℓΘ (θ) = log π
                                     eΘ (θ).                                       (49.3)

The tilde emphasizes that normalization is unnecessary.
   Euclidean HMC is efficient when typical posterior directions have comparable scales
and curvature. It can be inefficient when a single global mass matrix cannot accommo-
date strong correlations, changing curvature, funnels, or nonlinear ridges. A step size
small enough for the stiffest region then makes movement elsewhere slow. An affine

                                             481
482      CHAPTER 49. NEURAL TRANSPORT HAMILTONIAN MONTE CARLO

whitening map repairs constant covariance but cannot generally straighten changing ge-
ometry. NeuTra learns an explicit nonlinear coordinate map and runs ordinary HMC in
the learned coordinates.
   Three facts motivate the method and delimit its claims.
  1. The learned variational distribution need not be exact. Its purpose is to provide
     useful coordinates, not final posterior draws.
  2. The Jacobian-corrected HMC target is exact for the declared source-coordinate
     posterior whenever the frozen map is a bijection and HMC is implemented correctly.
  3. A poor map can still reduce efficiency or hide a mode from finite runs. Exact
     invariance is not a finite-time convergence guarantee.


49.2      Hamiltonian Monte Carlo from first principles
             e(q) on q ∈ Rd , introduce momentum p ∼ N (0, M ) with positive-definite
For a target π
mass M . Define

      U (q) = − log π
                    e(q),       K(p) = 12 p⊤ M −1 p,     H(q, p) = U (q) + K(p).    (49.4)

Hamilton’s equations are

                               q̇ = M −1 p,     ṗ = ∇q log π
                                                            e(q).                   (49.5)

Along an exact trajectory,
                     dH
                         = ∇q H ⊤ q̇ + ∇p H ⊤ ṗ                                    (49.6)
                      dt
                         = ∇U (q)⊤ M −1 p + (M −1 p)⊤ [−∇U (q)] = 0.                (49.7)

The phase-space velocity is v(q, p) = (∇p H, −∇q H), whose divergence is

                                  ∇q · ∇p H − ∇p · ∇q H = 0                         (49.8)

because the mixed derivatives cancel. Liouville’s formula therefore gives a unit Jacobian
determinant for the exact flow, so phase-space volume is preserved. If (q(t), p(t)) solves
the equations, then (q(−t), −p(−t)) does also, proving reversibility after a momentum
flip.
    Numerically, one leapfrog step of size ϵ is

                              pn+1/2 = pn + 2ϵ ∇ log π
                                                     e(qn ),                        (49.9)
                                                −1
                                qn+1 = qn + ϵM pn+1/2 ,                            (49.10)
                                pn+1 = pn+1/2 + 2ϵ ∇ log π
                                                         e(qn+1 ).                 (49.11)

Each substep is a shear: it changes one block while holding the other fixed, and therefore
has block-triangular Jacobian determinant one. Their composition is volume-preserving.
Replacing ϵ by −ϵ and reversing the substep order recovers the starting state; because
the kick–drift–kick order is symmetric, a momentum flip supplies the required proposal
reversibility. After L steps, the proposal (q ′ , −p′ ) is accepted with probability

                            α = min{1, exp[−H(q ′ , p′ ) + H(q, p)]}.              (49.12)
49.3. EXACT NEURAL CHANGE OF VARIABLES                                                 483

Indeed, for the joint density ρ(q, p) ∝ e−H(q,p) and the deterministic reversible proposal
map F , the accepted forward probability mass is
                                                                      
                    ρ(F x)                                         ρ(x)
      ρ(x) min 1,            = min{ρ(x), ρ(F x)} = ρ(F x) min 1,           ,       (49.13)
                     ρ(x)                                         ρ(F x)

where x = (q, p). This is detailed balance; the unit Jacobian means no proposal volume
factor is missing. The Metropolis correction therefore removes leapfrog discretization
bias. A high acceptance rate alone is not evidence of good exploration: ϵ can be so small
that proposals are nearly unchanged.


49.3      Exact neural change of variables
Let z ∈ Rd be latent HMC coordinates and let

                                          θ = Tϕ (z)                               (49.14)

be a differentiable bijection with frozen parameters ϕ. For a measurable set A in source
space,
                                     Z
                       Pr(Θ ∈ A) =      πΘ (θ) dθ                                (49.15)
                                     ZA

                                  =          πΘ (Tϕ (z))| det JTϕ (z)| dz.       (49.16)
                                      Tϕ−1 (A)


Therefore the pulled-back target is

                           π        eΘ (Tϕ (z))| det JTϕ (z)|,
                           eZ (z) = π                                              (49.17)
                           ℓZ (z) = ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + log | det JTϕ (z)|.              (49.18)

If a Markov kernel leaves πZ invariant, pushing its stationary draws through Tϕ produces
draws from πΘ . Hence approximation error in training does not change the stationary
posterior. It changes only the geometry, initialization, and finite-compute efficiency.
    By the chain rule, the latent score is

                  ∇z ℓZ (z) = JTϕ (z)⊤ ∇θ ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + ∇z log | det JTϕ (z)|.     (49.19)

Both terms are derivatives of the same scalar target. Dropping the log Jacobian changes
the probability measure; dropping its derivative gives the wrong force for that measure.
During HMC, ϕ is fixed, so no optimizer state participates in (49.19).
    Artifacts distinguish latent z, unconstrained source θ, and physical ϑ = C(θ). HMC
integrates z; the filter target consumes θ; scientific summaries use ϑ.


49.4      The historical BayesFilter dense IAF
The implementation and numerical settings in this section are historical and unfaithful to
the original author’s code. The current author-based IAF uses a free scale bias outside the
conditional cap and nonzero author initialization; see Section 50.8 and the implementation
