When heterogeneous physical units make identity initialization numerically unsuitable,
the final IAF output biases may be initialized so that the stack has Tϕpure (0) = c0 and its
leading diagonal scale is exp(s0 ). Both biases remain trainable members of ϕ; c0 and s0
are not serialized as a fixed affine chart and do not contribute an extra Jacobian term.
A bounded-scale recipe must strictly contain every entry of s0 ; the paper-style recipe
instead uses the MADE log-scale output directly, as in the reference implementation.
Applying this initialization at the final stage keeps the preceding IAFs in latent scale;
putting it at the first stage would make every later network consume heterogeneous
physical-unit activations. This warm start changes the optimizer’s initial state, not the
change-of-variables formula or the target density.


49.5      Reverse-KL training and its gradient
Let r(z) = N (0, I) and let qϕ be the pushforward distribution of θ = Tϕ (z). Change of
variables gives
                       log qϕ (Tϕ (z)) = log r(z) − log | det JT (z)|.          (49.28)
The normalized posterior is πΘ (θ) = π
                                     eΘ (θ)/Z. Thus
        KL(qϕ ∥πΘ ) = Ez∼r [log r(z) − log | det JT (z)| − ℓΘ (Tϕ (z))] + log Z.    (49.29)
Neither log r(z) nor log Z depends on ϕ, so the optimized loss is
                       L(ϕ) = −Ez∼r [ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + log | det JT (z)|] .             (49.30)
For a batch z (1:B) , the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator is the corresponding sample mean.
Reparameterization yields
                  ∇ϕ L = −Er JT,ϕ (z)⊤ ∇θ ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + ∇ϕ log | det JT (z)| .
                                                                           
                                                                                    (49.31)
This is differentiated through the same declared target used later by HMC.
    Reverse KL penalizes mass placed where the posterior density is low but may un-
derrepresent separated modes or tails. Consequently, heldout loss can select a training
recipe, and nonfinite loss or gradients can veto training, but loss cannot establish poste-
rior convergence. HMC corrects density error only if finite computation actually explores
all relevant latent regions.
    BayesFilter uses stateless Gaussian batches, one leading-batch target call, float64
TensorFlow/TFP, XLA, GPU memory growth, and Adam with bias correction. Gradient
clipping and learning-rate schedules are named-procedure choices: some procedures use
global-norm clipping and linear or piecewise decay, while the SSL–LSTM capacity families
use per-variable clipping and an explicitly controlled constant learning rate. The run
manifest must identify the exact choice; neither policy is a universal NeuTra default. No
NumPy or Python sample-axis loop belongs to the active training/HMC route. A valid
segmented resume restores weights, both Adam moments, completed step, seed schedule,
and learning-rate schedule.


49.6      When transport training learns scale but little
          nonlinear shape
The September 2026 q20 investigation asks why reverse-KL training can produce an al-
most affine map while substantial nonlinear posterior geometry remains. The target is
486       CHAPTER 49. NEURAL TRANSPORT HAMILTONIAN MONTE CARLO

the four-parameter, thirty-observation UKF approximate posterior of the SSL–LSTM
example. The “q20” designation refers to its latent-state configuration, not a twenty-
dimensional parameter vector. All statements in this section concern that specified ap-
proximate posterior; accurate sampling from it would not establish agreement with the
exact state-space posterior. The earlier three-stage examples in this chapter and the
two/four-stage q20 recipes are distinct experiments.


49.6.1     What failed, and what has already been checked
Let z ∼ r = N (0, I4 ), let θ = Tϕ (z), and define the unnormalized transformed log density
and its Gaussian-score residual as

          ℓZ (z) = ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + log | det JT (z)|,     g(z) = ∇z ℓZ (z) + z.       (49.32)

An exact Gaussianizing map has g = 0. A useful HMC map need not make this identity
exact, so the residual explains geometry and can nominate a repair; posterior estimation
still requires the sampling checks described elsewhere in this chapter.
     On the saved bank of 1,000 base-normal points, affine regressions explain 99.866–
99.999% P  of the coordinate variation of the depth-four map. Of the observed squared
residual n ∥g(z (n) )∥2 , 89.02% lies in latent coordinate 2. A constant-plus-linear regres-
sion on all four latent coordinates explains only 0.573% of that component’s residual
energy; its root-mean-square magnitude is 4.2638. That latent direction principally con-
trols the physical observation weight, approximately θ3 = 0.2743 + 0.4958z2 on this bank.
These descriptive observations localize a failure to learn nonlinear shape. They are not a
bound on derivatives of the fitted map, proof of separability, or evidence that the target
has multiple modes.
     The corresponding source audit checked the loss

                              −Er [ℓΘ (Tϕ (z)) + log | det JT (z)|]                 (49.33)

and verified that its first parameter derivative includes both the supplied analytic target
score and the log determinant. The previously checked finite differences do not support
a missing-score explanation. The reported loss near 43 is not a KL divergence of 43: the
additive terms Er log r + log Z are not included in that number.
    Clipping alone also cannot explain the remaining failure. The continuation control
clipped 99.02% of its updates, whereas the clipping repair clipped 0.68% and the depth-
four continuation clipped none. Each principal repair added 1,024 updates with batch
32. The added layers consequently have only 1,024 updates, and the existing layers
have 2,048 lifetime updates. The late depth-four losses are flat and noisy; improvement
from parent to endpoint does not establish continuing improvement at the endpoint or
optimizer convergence.
    These results and their frozen-source identities are preserved in the September 23
mathematical audit. They motivate three distinct mechanisms: release overall scale from
a saturating parameterization, reduce noise in the same reverse-KL gradient, and expose
direct scalar shape changes. The observations do not yet determine which mechanism
matters most.
49.6. WEAK NONLINEAR LEARNING IN Q20                                                   487

49.6.2     Why reverse-KL stationarity need not remove the score
           residual
The objective averages log density, whereas g measures its derivative. Even an exact
optimum within an affine family can retain nonlinear score error. Consider p(x) ∝
exp(−x4 /12) and x = m + σz. The nonconstant reverse-KL objective is

                                      m4 + 6m2 σ 2 + 3σ 4
                          L(m, σ) =                       − log σ.                 (49.34)
                                             12
For fixed positive σ, its minimum in m is zero. At m = 0, ∂σ L = σ 3 − σ −1 , so the
optimum is σ = 1. Nevertheless g(z) = z − z 3 /3, and the Gaussian moments give

                  E[g] = E[zg] = 0,       E[g 2 ] = 1 − 32 (3) + 19 (15) = 23 .    (49.35)

Thus affine directions can be stationary while nonlinear error remains. This is an analytic
example, not a fitted description of the q20 posterior.
   Adding E∥g∥2 to the objective would change the optimization problem. Its parameter
derivative generally requires derivatives of the target score, which the existing stopped-
score bridge does not supply. The following path-gradient mechanism instead preserves
reverse KL and needs only the first target score.

            ent
Write sq (θ) = ∇θ log qϕ (θ) and sπ (θ) = ∇θ ℓΘ (θ). With a differentiable full-support map

            ∇ϕ KL(qϕ ∥πΘ ) = Er (∂ϕ T )⊤ (sq − sπ ) + Eq ∂ϕ log qϕ (θ)|θ ,

          Eq ∂ϕ log qϕ (θ)|θ = ∂ϕ qϕ (θ) dθ = 0.                                       (49.40)

The path estimator retains the first expectation. At q = π it vanishes for each draw,
whereas the ordinary estimator can remain noisy. Removing a zero-mean term does not
guarantee lower variance away from the optimum, because covariance between terms also
matters [Roeder et al., 2017, Section 2]. A finite minibatch therefore need not give equal
standard and path gradients. Their expectations, rather than their pointwise values,
must be checked against the same objective.
   The proposal score can be obtained without numerical inversion. Differentiate the
change-of-variables identity at a known base draw:

                           log qϕ (Tϕ (z)) = log r(z) − log | det JT (z)|,             (49.41)
                             ⊤
                       JT (z) sq (Tϕ (z)) = −z − ∇z log | det JT (z)|.                 (49.42)

Solving this transposed-Jacobian system supplies sq . Applied one layer at a time it is the
score recursion of Vaitl et al. [2024, Proposition 3.2 and Appendix B.1]. Their optimized
coupling-flow timing results do not establish the cost of our autoregressive implementa-
tion. The first optional implementation uses a bounded small dense Jacobian assembled
by coordinate-wise vector-Jacobian products. That loop is over the four parameter co-
ordinates, not training samples; all sample rows remain batched. It uses no TensorFlow
pfor and makes no coupling-flow speed claim.

                                                                     P
respect to ϕ. This scalar carries the intended gradient but is not the reverse-KL loss; the
actual −ℓΘ − log | det JT | must be reported separately. Stopping the complete forward
log determinant would discard necessary terms. The inverse-density construction of Vaitl
et al. [2022] and the forward recursion above are two ways to compute the required
proposal score correctly.

                   JT⊤ (sq − sπ ) = −g,      ∇ϕ KL = −Er (JT−1 ∂ϕ T )⊤ g .

                                                                                       (49.43)

If available parameter variations have little projection onto g, the expected gradient
can be small despite large nonlinear error. Variance reduction helps resolve an existing
direction; it does not create a missing one.

conditioner also contribute; the scalar formula alone is not the entire multidimensional
score.
   NAF’s significant cost distinction is its inverse. Given y = τ (x), each component logit
crosses y at rk = (y − bk )/ak . Therefore
                                   min rk ≤ τ −1 (y) ≤ max rk .                         (49.51)
                                        k                        k
490       CHAPTER 49. NEURAL TRANSPORT HAMILTONIAN MONTE CARLO

At the lower bound every sigmoid is at most σ(y); at the upper bound every sigmoid
is at least σ(y), proving the bracket. A bounded bisection can solve inside it, with
explicit input/output tolerances, an iteration cap, and a failure result. Training in the
forward reverse-KL direction and ordinary latent HMC steps do not require this inverse on
every evaluation. Physical-space proposal densities, forward-KL training, and ensemble
cross densities can do so. Fast forward determinants consequently do not imply a cheap
complete ensemble pipeline. The first implementation does not differentiate through
bisection or offer inverse-based training.
    There is also an initialization trap. At ak = 1, bk = 0 for all components, with
w = softmax(η),
                         ∂ak τ = wk x,     ∂bk τ = wk , ∂ηk τ = 0.                (49.52)
The scalar parameter directions are initially only affine. Small distinct components expose
nonlinear directions, but their initial map displacement must be measured. Zero output
initialization is not generally a defect: successful NAF and Glow recipes start near identity
[Huang et al., 2018, Appendix E][Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018, Section 3.3]. The question
is whether the chosen features and parameter directions can respond usefully on this
target.
    The smallest shape experiment freezes the current map and uses Tψ = T0 ◦ Dψ , where
Dψ (z) = (z1 , τψ (z2 ), z3 , z4 ). It includes log τψ′ (z2 ) in the loss and keeps the posterior
unchanged. The observed concentration of error motivates coordinate 2, but does not
guarantee a marginal correction will suffice. Residual dependence on other coordinates
would motivate a conditional transform next.
    Explicit inverses are available for rational-quadratic splines, along with inexpensive
determinants [Durkan et al., 2019, Section 3]. Their usual construction is C 1 but generally
not C 2 . Since the scalar transformed force contains τ ′′ /τ ′ , knot behavior requires a sepa-
rate HMC energy and derivative check. They remain an alternative, not an automatically
qualified replacement.

49.6.6      How the three mechanisms will be distinguished
First test the arithmetic on analytic targets: affine identities, Gaussian pointwise can-
cellation of the path gradient, equality of expected standard and path gradients under
converged quadrature, finite differences of scalar values and log determinants, and in-
verse roundtrips including tails. Checkpoint reconstruction must preserve all mechanism
parameters and never imply HMC admission. Tiny CPU fixtures with hidden GPUs an-
swer these engineering questions only. A few successful optimizer steps are not training
evidence for the q20 posterior.
    The target experiment then starts from the same saved endpoint for isolated scale,
gradient-estimator, and scalar-shape arms, with unchanged reverse KL. An affine-only
scalar control distinguishes shape from location and scale. Pair the latent streams where
meaningful and charge actual worker time; equal target-row counts need not imply equal
optimizer steps or equal runtime. Keep true losses, per-block gradient/update measure-
ments, scale derivatives, inverse work where used, and checkpoints. A failed candidate
triggers the corresponding next repair; it does not alone reject NeuTra.
    Every numerical choice needs a local basis. The coordinate follows the saved residual
decomposition. The minimum nonlinear component count follows from K = 1 being
affine, but sufficient capacity is uncalibrated. Positive slopes and weights follow from
invertibility. Initial component spread is judged by map displacement and nonlinear
49.7. GEOMETRY INDUCED IN SOURCE SPACE                                                  491

response. Batch, learning rate, continuation length, replication, and any revised condi-
tional cap must be priced and calibrated on the actual target. Published values such as
the original NeuTra batch 4,096 and 5,000 updates are experimental settings, not q20
defaults.
    Fresh heldout objective estimates and the standard 1,000-point score report can sup-
port nomination. They cannot establish mode coverage, convergence, or superiority
among stochastic candidates without the corresponding evidence. A new scalar family
also requires supported frozen-map reconstruction, transformed-score checks, and fresh
public-tuner qualification before HMC. The implementation and experiment sequence is
recorded in the three-mechanism repair plan. The strongest competing explanation re-
mains that the current IAF family could learn adequate nonlinear shape under a better
calibrated continuation. The three tests are designed to distinguish that explanation from
limited effective parameter directions, rather than assume an architecture replacement is
necessary.

49.6.7     A shared implementation of the proposed mechanisms
The September 24 implementation makes the affine autoregressive map, its inverse, and
its score derivatives common to ordinary, weighted, legacy, and frozen-map consumers.
Historical checkpoints retain their original scale conventions. A separate source-based
IAF configuration implements the NeuTra author code’s conditional cap with a free bias
at every layer, together with the paper’s three-stage, two-hidden-layer ELU architecture.
The fixed cap is not a bound on the free global scale. The source initializer uses fan-in
variance scaling with factor 0.02, as selected by the author’s MakeIAFBijectorFn; neither
that factor nor the paper’s training schedule establishes a calibrated q20 protocol.
    The new DSF configuration is a full conditional neural autoregressive flow: the earlier
coordinates determine each coordinate’s positive slopes, shifts, and mixture weights. Its
source profile retains the author’s cMADE conditioner, final conditioner weight normaliza-
tion, and shared output projection, specialized to a constant context for an unconditional
target. The log-domain transformer preserves the paper’s full real support. It omits the
author implementation’s output shrinkage, which would bound that support. This nu-
merical distinction and the fixed random-number conventions are documented explicitly
in the implementation reference.
    Layerwise proposal-score propagation is connected to the Adam training update. It
uses Vaitl’s general score recursion and autoregressive triangular solves, not the coupling-
specific linear-cost formula. Inverse-density gradients use implicit differentiation of the
same conditional map. Training handoff includes the standard 1,000-point residual report;
a finite report alone establishes neither adequate whitening nor posterior convergence.
These changes close implementation gaps. Their numerical regression and GPU checks
are engineering evidence; a freshly calibrated q20 training run and downstream sampler
validation are still required.


49.7      Geometry induced in source space
NeuTra may also be understood as a learned position-dependent metric. With identity
latent mass, its Hamiltonian is

                       HZ (z, p) = −ℓΘ (T (z)) − log |J(z)| + 21 p⊤ p.              (49.53)
492      CHAPTER 49. NEURAL TRANSPORT HAMILTONIAN MONTE CARLO

Let J = JT (z) and define source momentum pθ = J −⊤ p. Then p = J ⊤ pθ and

                                   1 ⊤
                                   2
                                     p p = 12 p⊤    ⊤
                                               θ JJ pθ ,                             (49.54)
                               − log |J| = 12 log |(JJ ⊤ )−1 |.                      (49.55)

Hence the same scalar Hamiltonian in θ has metric

                                 G(θ) = (J(z)J(z)⊤ )−1 ,                             (49.56)

which explains how a nonlinear map adapts effective scale and orientation with position.
Unlike general Riemannian HMC, computation remains an explicit, separable Euclidean
HMC problem in z. The benefit exists only where the learned J approximates useful
posterior geometry.


49.8      Complete BayesFilter algorithm
For a valid batched target, the operational algorithm is:

  1. Define the physical model, prior, source chart, likelihood or filter-defined approx-
     imate likelihood, scalar log target, score, and target health telemetry. Verify val-
     ue/score and batch identity before training.

  2. Choose a fixed affine lift (c, L) and a small, target-specific candidate set of IAF
     widths and learning rates. Train each screen candidate with (49.30); compare on
     common heldout latent noise.

  3. Train a fresh final transport from independent initialization using the nominated
     recipe. Freeze and serialize its exact component order, weights, biases, masks, affine
     lift, target signature, and training-state hash.

  4. Construct (49.18) from the frozen map. Check trainable/frozen parity, finite values,
     scores, and target telemetry.

  5. Screen a broad set of fixed HMC pairs (ϵ, L) with disjoint seeds through the shared
     candidate controller. Acceptance evidence and numerical health qualify each ex-
     act pair; retain every verified member. Short-chain ESS and modern R-hat are
     reporting-only during kernel tuning.

  6. Retain warm-up chunks separately until the warm-up gate passes or the cap is
     reached. Never pool warm-up into posterior summaries.

  7. Accumulate fresh retained chunks until the joint R-hat, ESS, and health gates pass
     or the retained cap is reached.

  8. Transform retained z draws to source and physical coordinates and apply the prede-
     clared scientific diagnostic. Archive all three coordinates, seeds, settings, telemetry,
     hashes, and wall time.
49.9. SELECTING AMONG FROZEN TRANSPORTS                                                493

49.9      Selecting among frozen transports
Training restarts are candidate transports, not automatically permanent estimation arms.
After each transport has been frozen and independently bound to the same target, pre-
pare one immutable scope and run the shared candidate-set controller described in Sec-
tion 42.3. BayesFilter owns the fixed-kernel validation rungs, candidate-local rejection,
generic hard screens, and retention of every viable transport. The client owns training
receipts, transport provenance, and the declared score used to nominate among viable
candidates. A separate frozen transport is a separate scope; its states and verification
receipts never enter another scope’s queue.
    The recommended sequence is: freeze the transport and scope; measure the broad
fixed-kernel grid; validate every retained pair on fresh, disjoint seeds; create same-(L)
epsilon children only from typed directional evidence; verify each child independently;
retain all candidates that pass; and nominate one only after recording the score ordering
and its uncertainty status. A low reverse-KL or good whitening receipt can nominate
a candidate, but it does not prove global Gaussianity, posterior correctness, or sampler
superiority. R-hat belongs to separate posterior assessment and cannot reject, rank or
delay tuning members. An inconclusive result receives a declared evidence extension or
an explicit inconclusive disposition at its cap; it does not silently replace L.
    Do not rank restarts solely by training loss, silently discard viable candidates, or
treat a p-value as a universal quality score. The candidate receipt must say whether the
ordering is descriptive or statistically supported and must preserve the hard vetoes for
every rejected candidate.

The preserved-transition diagnostic API uses biased lag autocovariances, unbiased within-
chain variance and Geyer’s initial positive and monotone sequences, including the final
even-lag improvement used by Stan posterior and ArviZ. Its estimated integrated au-
tocorrelation time is bounded below by 1/ log10 (S) for S input draws. This finite-sample
safeguard prevents unstable negative ESS estimates; it is not a theoretical upper bound
on an antithetic chain’s true ESS. Constant pooled samples remain non-promotable.
    Bulk ESS uses split, rank-normalized draws. Tail ESS is the minimum of the split-
chain ESS values for the quantile-CDF indicators I(x ≤ q0.05 ) and I(x ≤ q0.95 ). The
latter complements I(x > q0.95 ), whereas an inclusive upper-tail indicator differs when
rejected proposals repeat a cutoff value. Linear percentile interpolation preserves equal
endpoints exactly. These are finite-run diagnostics, not proofs of convergence.
    The preserved-transition API
                               pretains its unsplit-chain convention for pooled posterior-
mean ESS and MCSE, SD(x)/ Neff,mean . Its per-chain MCSE uses the same estimator
with one chain. ArviZ’s public mean-ESS diagnostic instead splits chains, so a reference
comparison must state which convention it checks. Bulk/tail diagnostics still use split
chains. This reporting correction does not change HMC transitions or retroactively alter
archived diagnostic reports.
    The public rank_normalized_hmc_diagnostics entry point uses these same bulk/-
tail and split/folded R-hat implementations. Its inputs retain the order draw, chain,
parameter; the preserved-transition API uses chain, draw, parameter. Thresholds and
output schemas remain unchanged. The separately named TFP mean/quantile precision
option and the temporal-ESS heuristic used during covariance adaptation have their own
estimator conventions; this reporting repair does not change them.
    The historical case-study protocol below used four chains, warm-up modern R-hat
at most 1.05, retained modern R-hat at most 1.01, minimum bulk ESS 1000, minimum
tail ESS 400, and caps of 10,000 warm-up and retained draws per chain. The value 1000
is a conservative convenience rule, not a theorem. The structural result below missed
it narrowly and is labeled with the disclosed post-result owner adjudication rather than
called an automated pass.
    New posterior runs declare ESS and precision requirements using the assessment pol-
icy in Chapter 47. The rank and R-hat calculations have version bayesfilter.hmc_
diagnostic_math.v2; bulk and tail ESS use bayesfilter.stan_initial_positive_
monotone_ess.v1. Historical numerical reports below have not been recomputed with
these estimators and cannot establish current threshold passage.
    TFP’s fixed HamiltonianMonteCarlo kernel did not expose native divergence flags
for these runs. The preserved hard screen defines an energy failure as a nonfinite log
acceptance ratio or one below −1000. This narrower telemetry is reported honestly and
is not renamed as a native divergence diagnostic.

HMC and are therefore not counted.


49.15         Interpretation, failure modes, and nonclaims
The evidence supports the bounded statement that learned NeuTra has produced viable
transformed-HMC sampling across a broad set of difficult geometries, including exact
linear-Gaussian, nonlinear biological, epidemic, structural, hierarchical, regression, and
DSGE-derived targets. In the five comparable synthetic configurations, all 38 inspected
truths were non-extreme and inside empirical 95% intervals for one frozen dataset each.
    The strongest alternative explanations are favorable fixture choice, reverse KL missing
a mode not visited by finite HMC, approximate filter likelihoods defining a different
posterior from the exact scientific model, and heterogeneous historical protocols. The
results therefore do not establish:

       repeated-sampling calibration or 95% frequentist coverage;

       exactness of UKF, SGQF, or SVD-filter posteriors relative to the latent data-
        generating model;

       universal mode or tail recovery by reverse KL;

       statistical superiority over plain HMC, NUTS, RMHMC, or another map;

       convergence merely because R-hat and ESS cross finite thresholds;
49.15. INTERPRETATION, FAILURE MODES, AND NONCLAIMS                                    503

    universal architecture, optimizer, HMC, production, or default policy.

    The engineering, sampler, and scientific ledgers remain separate. A correct map can
train poorly; a low loss can yield bad HMC; valid HMC can place truth in an extreme
tail; and one-fixture success can fail under repeated datasets. That separation is not
procedural caution: it is the mathematical distinction between implementing the intended
density, exploring it adequately, and learning something scientifically defensible from the
resulting posterior.
Chapter 50

Modern Importance Sampling and
Coverage-Aware Flow Training

A posterior can have several economically distinct explanations of the same observations.
A proposal fitted around one explanation may generate smooth, well-behaved trajectories
while missing the others. Importance sampling makes this failure precise: a proposal must
assign sufficient probability wherever the posterior contributes to the expectation being
estimated. A tractable unnormalized posterior is enough to compute weights, but it does
not make unvisited regions visible. Modern methods address this difficulty by adapting
mixtures, moving through intermediate distributions, learning transport maps, or learn-
ing stochastic dynamics. Their common purpose is to make the change of probability
measure less variable.
                                                                                        d
                                                                              R x∈R .
    This chapter develops these ideas for a posterior on unconstrained parameters
Write its unnormalized density as γ(x), its normalizing constant as Z = γ(x) dx ∈
(0, ∞), and its normalized density as p(x) = γ(x)/Z. In a state-space application, γ
includes the prior, likelihood and any parameter-chart Jacobian. If a filter supplies an
approximate likelihood, all subsequent identities concern that declared approximate pos-
terior. Learning a better proposal cannot remove the filter approximation.

A small mismatch repeated across many coordinates can therefore produce exponential

    A related sample-size analysis is due to Chatterjee and Diaconis [2018, Theorems
1.1–1.2]. They connect the threshold to exp{DKL (p∥q)}. Their bounds involve the con-
centration of log(p/q) under p and the integrand, with a separate self-normalized result.
The statement is not an unconditional rule that exactly exp(DKL ) samples suffice. It ex-
plains why the posterior’s typical set can be extremely rare under a superficially plausible
proposal. The second-moment identity above and the KL threshold answer related but
distinct questions: variance control and the onset of typical-set coverage.
    Modes alone do not determine probabilities. At an isolated interior mode mk with
positive-definite Hk = −∇2 log γ(mk ), the local quadratic approximation is

 γ(x) ≃ γ(mk ) exp{− 21 (x − mk )⊤ Hk (x − mk )},        ZkLap = γ(mk )(2π)d/2 |Hk |−1/2 . (50.8)
506                                  CHAPTER 50. MODERN IMPORTANCE SAMPLING

The determinant measures local volume. Ranking modes by height discards it. Even the
Laplace mass can fail for curved ridges, boundaries, heavy tails or nonquadratic basins.
Multistart optimization and mode merging, as developed within the adaptive multimodal
MCMC framework of Pompe et al. [2020, Section 2.2], provide useful candidate locations.
Finding all modes of an unrestricted nonlinear density remains a separate problem. A
finite optimizer search cannot establish exhaustiveness.
    A proposal does not need one component per mode. In a product of d/2 double-
well densities, the number of modes is 2d/2 , while the formula for the density remains
short. Exploiting structure can be far more economical than enumerating modes. This
distinction is central to interpreting high-dimensional multimodal demonstrations.

           mixtures

approximations. Given weighted locations, a normalized kernel estimate has the form

corresponding multiple-importance or sequential weighting; retroactively dividing all old
draws by the latest proposal is not automatically correct.

50.4. DEFENSIVE AND ADAPTIVE PROPOSALS                                                   507

Jensen’s inequality applied to the latent component label gives the EM lower bound;
maximizing it yields these weighted moments. The weights remain fixed during each
empirical EM fit. Cappé et al. [2008, Section 2] derive adaptive updates for general
mixture classes. Covariance regularization, component removal and stopping remain
numerical choices; none creates evidence about an unvisited region.
    Raftery and Bao [2010, Section 3] develops incremental mixture importance sampling
(IMIS). It adds local Gaussian components near points with large importance weights,
estimates local covariance from neighboring points, simulates new draws and recomputes
weights against the resulting proposal mixture. It was designed for difficult epidemiolog-
ical posteriors, including nonlinear ridges. Its residual-weight trigger identifies where the
current sampled proposal is inadequate; it cannot add a component at a region that no
search or sample has reached.
    MitISEM replaces unrestricted kernel proliferation with adaptive Student-t mixtures
and importance-weighted EM [Hoogerheide et al., 2012, Sections 2 and 5; Appendix A].
For one tν (m, Σ) component, the Gaussian scale-mixture representation adds a latent
precision with conditional mean (ν + d)/(ν + (x − m)⊤ Σ−1 (x − m)). This supplies robust
weighted location and scatter updates. More explicitly, with τik = (νk + d)/(νk + δik ) and
δik = (Xi − mk )⊤ Σ−1k (Xi − mk ), one EM step at fixed νk gives

Here Σk is a scatter parameter, not the covariance; for νk > 2 the covariance is νk Σk /(νk −
2). Optimizing the degrees of freedom adds a scalar nonlinear update involving the latent
precision’s expected logarithm. Large-weight points motivate extra components. The
partial MitISEM extension factors marginal and conditional distributions, reducing the
dimension of each approximation problem when that factorization is useful. The locally
inspected source is the 2011 working paper preceding the 2012 publication; its extra
sequential, permutation and partial-mixture constructions should be distinguished from
a claim to reproduce every published experiment.


50.4       Defensive and adaptive proposals
A defensive mixture protects against a fitted proposal becoming too narrow:

                      qλ (x) = (1 − λ)qfit (x) + λq0 (x),   0 < λ ≤ 1.               (50.16)

If p(x) ≤ Cq0 (x) everywhere, then p/qλ ≤ C/λ and
                                  Z 2       Z
                                    p     C       C
                                       ≤      p= .                                   (50.17)
                                    qλ    λ       λ
The domination assumption is the substantive protection; the word “heavy-tailed” by
itself is insufficient. A very small λ can still make finite-sample exploration ineffective.
    Delyon and Portier [2021, Theorems 7–9] study a kernel estimate mixed with a safe
density and give convergence and integral-estimation results under conditions on domina-
tion, bandwidth and the declining safe share. Their root-N integral asymptotics concern
508                            CHAPTER 50. MODERN IMPORTANCE SAMPLING

increasing sample size at fixed dimension under the stated regularity assumptions. They
do not remove the bandwidth’s dimension dependence or guarantee small finite-sample
cost in high dimension. For example, the related regularized safe scheme of Korba and
Portier [2022] requires, among its conditions, λn → 0, hn → 0 and log n/(nhdn λn ) → 0. It
also requires q0 ≥ cp, boundedness and regularity of the density and kernel, and controls
such as (1−ηn ) log hn → 0 when powered weights are used. The factor hdn shows explicitly
where dimension remains in the convergence requirements.
    Korba and Portier [2022, Sections 2–3] regularize importance weights using an expo-
nent η ∈ (0, 1]. The population calculation is
                                         η
                                     p(x)
                              q(x)           = p(x)η q(x)1−η .                     (50.18)
                                     q(x)
Lower η reduces concentration but changes the distribution fitted by those weights. Their
mirror-descent interpretation and safe kernel mixture balance this bias against variance,
with asymptotic conditions driving η toward one. Regularized adaptation and final esti-
mation are different operations: an estimate of Ep f still requires weights for p, unless a
different estimand is explicitly intended.
    Gradient-based adaptive importance samplers (GRAMIS) use target gradients, local
curvature and interactions among proposal components to direct an adaptive mixture
[Elvira et al., 2023, Section 3 and Table 2]. Local preconditioning can move a com-
ponent toward a high-density region; repulsion reduces redundant concentration. Their
samples retain evaluable proposal densities and importance correction. For equally al-
located
      PMsamples from M proposals, their deterministic-mixture weight denominator is
   −1
M       j=1 qj (x), so every sampled point is judged against the entire current proposal
mixture. The mean update combines a backtracked preconditioned score step with re-
pulsion:                                                       X
                            m+i = m i + θi Σ i ∇ log γ(m i ) +   rij .              (50.19)
                                                         j̸=i

The paper specifies the scaling of rij from a Poisson-field construction and a distance-
dependent interaction. Backtracking tests the score step without the repulsion term, and
the covariance uses local negative inverse Hessian information only when positive definite-
ness permits it, retaining valid prior information otherwise. Thus the method is not an
unconditional Newton step through an indefinite Hessian. The reported high-dimensional
banana examples exploit strong structure. Such examples support investigation of the
mechanism, not unrestricted mode discovery in every 50-dimensional posterior.
    Gaussian-mixture variational inference (GMMVI) addresses another objective. Arenz
et al. [2023, Sections 2–4 and Appendix A] unify natural-gradient updates, trust regions,
sample reuse and component adaptation for DKL (q∥p). A natural gradient has the form
−F (η)−1 ∇η DKL , where F is the Fisher information in the chosen variational coordinates.
It accounts for how parameter changes alter distributions. Reverse KL still weights errors
under q, so efficient optimization does not itself prevent missing modes. The paper’s warn-
ing that ELBO-based tuning can impair other distributional metrics is directly relevant
to evaluating a learned transport.

The last mutation can be omitted, in which case f is evaluated at XK−1 . To see the
identity, suppose the weighted marginal before stage k is γk−1 (x) dx. Multiplication
changes it to γk (x) dx. Integrating the next state against Kk preserves this measure by
invariance. Induction from q0 proves the result. An equivalent path-density derivation
uses reverse kernels; it does not require each finite chain to reach equilibrium [Neal,
2001]. It does require correct invariance and support. Adapting a kernel from the same
interacting batch needs separate justification and must not silently inherit the fixed-kernel
unbiasedness statement.
    Log weights accumulate as a sum, avoiding products that overflow. For the geometric
bridge the increment is (βk − βk−1 )[log γ(Xk−1 ) − log q0 (Xk−1 )]. A small temperature
change limits the immediate variation of this increment. Good mutation is still neces-
sary: many intermediate densities with negligible movement can preserve a bad particle
configuration at high cost.
    Sequential Monte Carlo adds resampling. Given normalized weights, draw parent
indices with those probabilities, reset weights appropriately and apply mutation. Condi-
tional unbiasedness of the resampling operation preserves the weighted measure in expec-
tation. Products of the incremental normalizer estimates give the usual SMC normalizer
estimator under standard fixed-design conditions [Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos, 2020].
Resampling trades weight degeneracy for dependence and possible loss of ancestry. It
cannot manufacture a mode that neither the initial particles nor mutation reach.


50.6       Annealed flow transport and continual training
A learned bijection Tk can move particles before they are weighted. If X ∼ πk−1 , change
of variables gives the incremental factor

                                       γk (Tk (X))| det DTk (X)|
                            Gk (X) =                             .                   (50.21)
                                                γk−1 (X)

Multiplying the pushed-forward law by this factor produces (Zk /Zk−1 )πk . Approximation
error in the map affects weight variance; a missing Jacobian changes the measure.
    AFT learns each map by minimizing a local reverse KL. Substituting the density of
Tk (X) into that KL yields, up to log Zk − log Zk−1 ,

        Lk (Tk ) = Eπk−1 [log γk−1 (X) − log γk (Tk (X)) − log | det DTk (X)|].      (50.22)

Arbel et al. [2021, Equations 7–9 and Algorithm 1] combine transport, importance cor-
rection, resampling and MCMC mutation. Their law of large numbers and central limit
theorem require explicit smoothness, moment and bounded-weight conditions, with fur-
ther assumptions for the CLT. Data-dependent fitted maps cannot simply be treated
as deterministic maps when asserting finite-sample unbiasedness; the paper supplies an
asymptotic analysis for its adaptive scheme.
510                                CHAPTER 50. MODERN IMPORTANCE SAMPLING

    CRAFT repeatedly runs the annealed SMC procedure and uses renewed particle ap-
proximations to update the stage maps [Matthews et al., 2022, Equation 5, Algorithms
1–3 and supplement]. Replenishing particles avoids optimizing each stage indefinitely
against one small fixed cloud. The maps learn progressively while corrected particles still
represent the annealed sequence. This is a different training organization from fitting
one whole-target flow by forward KL or FAB. Its practical advantage depends on target
cost, number of stages and mutation; neither repeated fitting nor the transport correction
eliminates finite-particle mode loss. One complete pass therefore starts with a fresh base
cloud, computes each stage’s current weighted training loss, moves points with the cur-
rent map, updates their weights using (50.21), resamples when the declared criterion calls
for it, and mutates with the intermediate target. The next pass uses the updated maps.
Optimizer updates and particle transport must follow the chosen algorithm’s ordering; a
map fitted using a particle cloud cannot be silently replaced in the weight denominator
by a later map.

Differentiation acts only on the final log density. Differentiating through the AIS trajec-

    The target gt changes when qt changes. Fitting a single frozen gt to completion is
therefore not the adaptive FAB procedure. New AIS passes and corrected replay retain
the connection to the current objective. At the ideal solution q = p, g = p and the
auxiliary emphasis disappears.

50.7.1     Replay corrections and their limits
Suppose a stored AIS point was weighted for γ 2 /qold . The corresponding unnormalized
target ratio is
                     γ(x)2 /qϕ (x)    qold (x)
          cϕ (x) =       2
                                    =          ,   log cϕ = log qold − log qϕ .       (50.31)
                     γ(x) /qold (x)    qϕ (x)
Store the point, its AIS log weight and the log density used for that weight. Sam-
ple replay
        P indices proportional to their stored weights, then use the minibatch loss
     −1
−B        i stopgrad(ci ) log qϕ (Xi ). Before the optimizer changes ϕ, add log ci to each se-
lected priority and replace its stored log density by the currently evaluated one. Successive
corrections telescope: (qa /qb )(qb /qc ) = qa /qc .
    This is Algorithm 1 and Section 3.2 of Midgley et al. [2023]. It saves expensive
posterior evaluations because old points need only a new flow density. It does not permit
uniform sampling from the buffer followed by the same correction: that would omit
the original AIS priorities. Likewise, inserting detached corrections into a trainer that
automatically renormalizes every minibatch changes the stated replay loss.
    The paper’s practical sampling without replacement introduces bias. The inspected
author JAX implementation additionally caps ci in the loss, with a configurable default
of ten, while refreshing stored log priorities with the uncapped correction. Capping
bounds a stochastic update but changes its expectation. Its activation frequency and
effect require measurement. Pooled replay, finite AIS, stale priorities and dependence
are further reasons not to call practical replay gradients exactly unbiased. A useful
implementation must preserve the distinction between the underlying objective and its
finite training procedure.

50.7.2     Tail integrability is stronger than full support
A Gaussian example demonstrates the issue. If p = N (0, σp2 ) and q = N (0, σq2 ), then

                       p(x)2
                                                      
                                           2   1     1
                             = C exp −x           −           .                     (50.32)
                       q(x)                    σp2 2σq2

Its integral is finite precisely when σq2 > σp2 /2. Both densities have full support even
when this condition fails. A highly contracted reverse-KL warm start may therefore
create an invalid FAB auxiliary density. Radial evaluations and weight diagnostics can
expose trouble but cannot prove a global tail bound. A defensive mixture with a proved
dominating component can guarantee a finite second moment by (50.17); it also changes
the proposal family and must be accounted for explicitly.
    FAB’s Appendix C studies favorable dimensional scaling under factorized p, q, inde-
pendent coordinate parameters and perfect intermediate transitions. Its gradient-variance
calculation motivates increasing intermediate steps with dimension. It is not a guaran-
tee for arbitrary dependent posteriors with local HMC. The 32-dimensional Many-Well
benchmark has 65,536 modes through a product construction; it demonstrates exploita-
tion of structure, not an exhaustive optimizer search over arbitrary modes.


50.8       Combining FAB with IAF and NeuTra
FAB supplies the training procedure; an inverse autoregressive flow supplies the density
family. For stage input z, use

         uj = zj exp{sj (z<j )} + µj (z<j ),    sj = bj + c tanh{hj (z<j )/c}.     (50.33)

Masked neural networks ensure that sj and µj depend only on preceding coordinates.
The free bias bj lies outside the conditional cap. This is the option in Hoffman’s author
code used by the current BayesFilter IAF; the conditional contribution is bounded, while
the complete log scale need not be. The cap c = 2, width sixteen and four-parameter
application are local choices. The source architecture uses ELU conditioners, author
block masks, nonzero variance-scaled kernels and coordinate reversal between three stages
[Hoffman et al., 2019, Section 4.1.1 and accompanying code].
P The Jacobian of each stage is triangular with diagonal exp(sj ), hence log | det Df | =
   j sj . For a composition Tϕ with a fixed invertible outer affine map a + Az, stage
log determinants add and the affine contributes log | det A|. With standard-normal base
density φd ,
                         qϕ (x) = φd (Tϕ−1 (x))| det DTϕ (Tϕ−1 (x))|−1 .           (50.34)
Sampling evaluates each autoregressive stage in parallel across its coordinates. Evaluating
the density at an arbitrary x requires inversion: first recover z1 , then use it to recover
z2 , and continue. The diagonal solve is zj = [uj − µj (z<j )] exp[−sj (z<j )]. There is
no dense determinant, but FAB makes the inverse cost more prominent than reverse-KL
training does. Batches remain parallel; the coordinate dependency is intrinsic to this IAF
orientation. A nonlinear NAF [Huang et al., 2018] is a different scalar transformation
and is not required to combine FAB with IAF.
     At fixed x, implicit differentiation of Tϕ (z) = x gives

                                ∂ϕ z = −[Dz Tϕ (z)]−1 ∂ϕ Tϕ (z).                   (50.35)
50.9. STEIN METHODS AND STOCHASTIC TRANSPORT                                           513

Therefore the parameter gradient of log qϕ (x) = log φd (z) − log | det Dz Tϕ (z)| includes
both explicit parameter dependence and dependence through z. Holding this inverse
latent value fixed would omit terms. Autodifferentiating the native inverse recursion
computes this total derivative without materializing a dense Jacobian. Finite differences
of selected parameter directions provide an independent check. FAB’s detached x is fully
compatible with differentiating z = Tϕ−1 (x) with respect to ϕ.
    Once training is complete, freeze ϕ and define the NeuTra target

                 peZ (z) = γ(Tϕ (z))| det DTϕ (z)|,                                (50.36)
          ∇z log peZ (z) = DTϕ (z)⊤ ∇x log γ(Tϕ (z)) + ∇z log | det DTϕ (z)|.      (50.37)

Changing variables shows that an invariant chain for this density pushes forward to p,
regardless of how accurately qϕ approximates p. Identity latent mass is a valid choice;
mass adaptation is not a prerequisite. The auxiliary FAB target γ 2 /q never replaces the
posterior in this formula. Better importance-weight coverage may still coexist with sharp
latent curvature, so training success does not establish efficient HMC.
    For a perfectly Gaussianized posterior, ∇z log peZ (z) = −z and r(z) = log peZ (z) +
∥z∥2 /2 is constant. The standard post-training check evaluates the score residual and r on
one thousand fresh normal-base points, preserving finite/status failures and the residual
distribution. This checks geometry where the map generates points. Independent region
occupancy and target-weighted evidence are needed for coverage; full retained chains and
their uncertainty diagnostics are needed for posterior estimation.

Stein variational gradient descent uses kernels in a different role from a kernel mixture

    Projected SVGD exploits a likelihood-informed subspace [Chen and Ghattas, 2020].
A sensitivity matrix built from likelihood scores identifies directions where the posterior
differs most strongly from the prior. For a Gaussian prior with covariance C, one common
form is
                H = Ep [(∇ log L(X))(∇ log L(X))⊤ ],       Hψj = λj C −1 ψj ,      (50.40)
where L is the likelihood and the eigenvectors are orthonormal in the prior precision
metric. The associated optimal conditional-expectation approximation averages L over
discarded prior coordinates. Under the functional-inequality and prior assumptions used
514                                CHAPTER 50. MODERN IMPORTANCE SAMPLING

in that literature, its KL approximation error is controlled by a constant times j>r λj .
This statement concerns the projected target approximation; finite particles and varia-
tional training add errors of their own. It is not a bound on an arbitrary implementation
merely using the top r eigenvectors. The method transports coordinates in that subspace
and represents the complement using the prior conditional structure. Its error bounds
depend on assumptions and the neglected eigenvalue tail. If many directions are strongly
informed, projection has little advantage; nominal dimension alone does not determine
its suitability.

The intermediate densities telescope; integration of the backward transitions leaves ter-
minal density γK . For nondegenerate Euler diffusion steps, the Fk are Gaussian and can
be evaluated. Continuous-time versions use Radon–Nikodym derivatives between path
measures under the requisite absolute-continuity and integrability conditions. The SCLD
paper derives these weights and trains controls using subtrajectory log-variance losses,
including off-policy sampling. An additive unknown log normalizer disappears from a
variance. For a detached reference path law Rn with sufficient support, the subtrajectory
objective has the form

               Ln (ϕ) = VarRn [log Wn,ϕ ] = ERn [(log Wn,ϕ − ERn log Wn,ϕ )2 ].                  (50.44)

With the reference law held fixed while differentiating, its gradient is 2ERn [(log Wn,ϕ −
ERn log Wn,ϕ )∇ϕ log Wn,ϕ ]. The centering term’s derivative cancels because the centered
50.10. EVALUATION AND IMPLEMENTATION                                                    515

log weight has mean zero. Off-policy training separates the sampling law from the con-
trol being updated. Section 2.3 and Theorem A.2 explain this loss and its off-policy use.
Proposition 2.3 instead establishes an exponential relative-error lower bound for a partic-
ular KL estimator on product path measures, motivating the alternative. Zero empirical
variance on a finite buffer is not equality of complete path measures. Resampling between
segments limits concentration over a whole long path, while optional MCMC refinement
improves terminal locations.
    A weighted path sampler is not automatically a tractable terminal density q(x). It
can provide training samples, but distilling them into an IAF is an additional approxima-
tion. SCLD’s reported multimodal examples include a 50-dimensional, forty-component
mixture. Its 1,600-dimensional log-Gaussian Cox example is primarily evaluated through
an ELBO; it is not evidence of exhaustive unknown-mode coverage in 1,600 dimensions.


50.10       Evaluation and implementation
The broad evaluation of Blessing et al. [2024, Sections 7–8 and Appendices D–F] com-
pares eleven variational and sampling methods across synthetic and Bayesian targets.
Its mixture examples vary dimension, including 2, 50 and 200, and show that strong
performance on an ELBO or one weight diagnostic can coexist with poor coverage. The
evidence depends on the authors’ architectures, tuning and budgets; it establishes no uni-
versal winner. It supports using several measurements that answer different questions.
    For a learned posterior proposal, correctness of density and derivatives comes first.
Next, inspect region coverage using independent information where available, importance-
weight reliability on untouched draws, and consistency across seeds. For a NeuTra map,
inspect transformed scores, numerical validity and downstream mixing. An apparently
superior extreme quantile from a short run is descriptive until its uncertainty is assessed.
A short successful test can retain a candidate; it cannot establish a production training
protocol.
    The author-maintained fab-jax repository separates sampling, replay and training
from its bundled coupling-layer flow. Its MIT license permits adaptation with the notice
retained. BayesFilter ports those FAB components to TensorFlow while keeping the
existing IAF and batch-native posterior evaluator. This preserves a single transport
implementation and avoids a second target implementation solely for a different autodiff
backend. The port follows the paper’s normalized-weight sum in (50.30); the inspected
JAX no-replay function takes a mean of those weighted terms, adding a factor 1/N .
The replay loss, correction cap and without-replacement choice are recorded separately.
These are explicit source differences, not interchangeable normalizations under arbitrary
optimizer settings.
    Three remaining costs determine the application. First, AIS requires repeated pos-
terior evaluations, with scores at every intermediate HMC step or values alone for a
Metropolis mutation. Second, IAF density evaluation at arbitrary points requires au-
toregressive inversion. Third, replay initialization must provide enough distinct points
to avoid fitting a tiny static cloud. The author’s recommendation is to use as few an-
nealing and mutation steps as can make the resulting samples usefully better than the
flow’s initial samples, then calibrate on the actual problem. An example configuration is
a starting hypothesis. Source faithfulness reduces accidental algorithm changes; target-
specific measurement determines whether the resulting training procedure is affordable
and scientifically useful.
Chapter 51

Metropolis-Corrected Neural-Force
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

This chapter studies a tempting acceleration of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for state-space
models. A filtering likelihood and its score may require one complete recursion through
the observations. Ordinary HMC calls that score at every leapfrog kick. A learned force
can make the interior trajectory cheap; one then evaluates the declared filtering posterior
at the proposed endpoint and applies a Metropolis correction.
    That summary is attractive but incomplete. A true endpoint posterior value does not
correct an arbitrary neural proposal. The simple HMC acceptance formula is valid only
after the proposal map has the required discrete reversibility and volume properties, and
its endpoint energy must include the final momentum. A stochastic filtering likelihood
adds a separate target problem: a fresh particle-filter estimate is not a deterministic
potential and cannot be inserted naively into that formula.
    The chapter therefore does four things. It derives a sufficient construction for a
frozen learned force, proves its invariant target, identifies precisely why broader learned-
Hamiltonian constructions need additional proof or correction, states the filtering bound-
ary for every relevant target class, and ends with an implementation and validation
contract for BayesFilter. The presentation is self-contained. The proposal of Dhulipala
et al. [2022] and its official implementation motivate the audit, but no theorem below
depends on accepting that paper’s stationarity argument.


51.1      The computational question
Let u ∈ Rd be unconstrained sampler coordinates and let y1:T denote the observations.
For a deterministic filtering backend F , define

            ℓF (u) = log p(u) + log LF (y1:T | u) + J(u),     UF (u) = −ℓF (u),      (51.1)

where J contains every parameter-transform log Jacobian. The subscript F is essential.
If F is a Kalman filter, LF may be the exact likelihood of the declared linear Gaussian
model. If F is a UKF or fixed SGQF, LF is normally an approximate filtering likelihood.
In either case, (51.1) is a deterministic scalar once the model, data, numerical branch,
and filter settings are frozen.
    With mass matrix M ≻ 0, ordinary HMC uses

                    HF (u, p) = UF (u) + K(p),       K(p) = 21 p⊤ M −1 p,            (51.2)

                                            516
51.2. PHASE-SPACE METROPOLIS CORRECTION                                                  517

and repeatedly evaluates ∇UF . Write CV for one new evaluation of UF , CG for one
evaluation of ∇UF together with whatever value the implementation returns, and CS for
one learned-force call. For L leapfrog steps, the leading proposal costs are approximately

                                  Cordinary ≃ LCG ,                                   (51.3)
                                   Cneural ≃ LCS + CV .                               (51.4)

The current state’s true value can be cached, so the corrected neural proposal usually
needs only one new endpoint value. Equations (51.3)–(51.4) are accounting identities, not
speedup theorems: acceptance, autocorrelation, fallback, training, compilation, batching,
and device utilization determine actual ESS per second.
Proposition 51.1 (When a neural-force proposal can reduce filtering work). Suppose or-
dinary and neural-force kernels use the same number L of interior steps. Ignore one-time
compilation and training, and suppose each kernel produces the same effective sample size
per accepted transition. Then the neural-force kernel has lower leading cost per transition
exactly when
                                   LCS + CV < LCG .                                  (51.5)
If training costs Ctrain and the per-transition saving is ∆C = LCG − (LCS + CV ) > 0, at
least Ctrain /∆C transitions are required to amortize training under these assumptions.
Proof. Subtract (51.4) from (51.3). The neural route is cheaper precisely when the dif-
ference ∆C is positive. After N transitions the accumulated saving is N ∆C; it covers
training if and only if N ∆C ≥ Ctrain .
    The equal-efficiency premise in Proposition 51.1 is deliberately strong. A useful ex-
periment must instead compare ESS per wall-clock second after charging training and
fallback. The proposition only explains why expensive filtering scores make the method
worth investigating.


51.2       Phase-space Metropolis correction
The target of one HMC transition is the joint density
                                          −1
                             ρF (u, p) = ZH  exp{−HF (u, p)}.                         (51.6)

Marginalizing p recovers the posterior proportional to e−UF (u) . Before each transition,
momentum is refreshed from N (0, M ). Proposal validity is easiest to state for a deter-
ministic phase-space map.
   Let R(u, p) = (u, −p) be the momentum flip. Let Φ be a differentiable bijection of
phase space and define the proposal map F = R ◦ Φ. The following proposition gives the
exact conditions behind the familiar HMC acceptance probability.
Proposition 51.2 (Deterministic involutive Metropolis proposal). Assume F : R2d →
R2d is a differentiable involution, F ◦ F = I, and | det DF (x)| = 1 for every x. From
state x = (u, p), propose x′ = F (x) and accept with

            α(x) = min{1, ρF (x′ )/ρF (x)} = min{1, exp[−HF (x′ ) + HF (x)]}.         (51.7)

Then the accept/reject kernel is reversible with respect to ρF and hence leaves ρF invariant.
518                                               CHAPTER 51. NEURAL-FORCE HMC

Proof. For any measurable sets A, B, the accepted flow from A to B is
    Z                               Z
        ρF (x)α(x)1{F (x) ∈ B} dx =    min{ρF (x), ρF (F x)}1{F (x) ∈ B} dx.         (51.8)
      A                                     A

Change variables y = F (x). Involution gives x = F (y) and the unit-Jacobian assumption
gives dx = dy. The expression becomes
                        Z
                           min{ρF (F y), ρF (y)}1{F (y) ∈ A} dy,                  (51.9)
                          B

which is the accepted flow from B to A. Rejections remain at the same state and are
automatically balanced. Thus detailed balance holds. Taking A to be the full state space
proves invariance.
Remark 51.1 (Terms in the endpoint correction). Equation (51.7) contains K(p′ ) −
K(p) as well as UF (u′ ) − UF (u). A correction based only on ℓF (u′ ) − ℓF (u) is generally
wrong. Momentum cancels only for a proposal that preserves kinetic energy exactly, which
ordinary leapfrog does not guarantee.
Proposition 51.3 (Omitting endpoint kinetic energy is wrong in general). There exist
volume-preserving involutive proposals for which the position-only acceptance
                         αU (x) = min{1, exp[−UF (u′ ) + UF (u)]}                   (51.10)
does not leave (51.6) invariant.
Proof. Take d = 1, UF (u) = u2 /2, K(p) = p2 /2, and the involution F (u, p) = (p, u). Its
Jacobian determinant is −1. Because HF (F x) = HF (x), the correct acceptance is one.
The position-only rule is min{1, exp[−p2 /2 + u2 /2]} and rejects a set of positive Gaussian
measure, for example whenever |p| > |u|. The reverse move from (p, u) uses the reciprocal
position ratio. The accepted forward mass is proportional to
                                    2   2             2    2
                                e−(u +p )/2 min{1, e(u −p )/2 },                    (51.11)
while the accepted reverse mass is proportional to
                                    2   2             2    2
                                e−(u +p )/2 min{1, e(p −u )/2 }.                    (51.12)
They differ whenever |u| ̸= |p|, so detailed balance fails. The missing kinetic term is
therefore not optional.


51.3      A sufficient learned-force construction
The cleanest construction learns only a position potential U

Remark 51.2 (Conservative learning is useful but not required for this proof). Writ-
ing gϕ = ∇U bϕ guarantees a conservative learned force and permits scalar value/gradient
training. The shear and reversibility proof above actually needs only a frozen position-
only gϕ . The stronger potential representation remains preferable because it constrains
learning, supports energy diagnostics, and prevents accidental momentum dependence.
Proposition 51.5 (Surrogate error affects efficiency, not this invariant target). Under
Proposition 51.4, replacing gϕ by any other fixed finite position-only force does not change
the invariant target. However, if the resulting proposal has large true energy error ∆HF =
HF (F x) − HF (x) on typical states, its acceptance is small for positive ∆HF , so it can
have arbitrarily poor efficiency.
Proof. The invariance proof uses only the map properties, not equality between gϕ and
∇UF . Acceptance is min{1, e−∆HF }. For any B > 0, states with ∆HF ≥ B have
acceptance at most e−B . Thus invariance does not bound mixing away from zero.

51.4      Limits of the broader learned-Hamiltonian ar-
          gument
The method in Dhulipala et al. [2022] learns a scalar Hamiltonian from both position
and momentum, obtains its vector field by differentiation, advances that field using a
synchronized-leapfrog formula, and applies a true endpoint Hamiltonian test. Its Sec-
tions 3.2–3.3 and Algorithms 3.2–3.3 are the relevant source anchors. The paper appeals
to Liouville’s theorem and observed forward/reverse trajectories. Those facts do not by
themselves prove the discrete proposal required by Proposition 51.2.
    The issue is mathematical, not terminological. There are three different claims:

  1. a Hamiltonian vector field has zero divergence and its exact flow preserves phase
     volume;

  2. an exact Hamiltonian flow is reversible under momentum flip only when the Hamil-
     tonian has the appropriate momentum symmetry;

  3. a numerical map must itself be volume-preserving and reversible, or its actual pro-
     posal/Jacobian terms must enter MH.

None of these claims implies the next without additional assumptions.

Proposition 51.6 (Liouville volume preservation does not prove time reversal). There
are smooth Hamiltonians whose exact flows preserve phase volume but are not reversible
under R(u, p) = (u, −p).

Proof. Take one dimension and
                           b p) = 1 u2 + 1 p2 + cp,
                           H(u,                               c ̸= 0.             (51.23)
                                  2      2

Hamilton’s equations are u̇ = p + c and ṗ = −u. Their vector field has divergence
∂u (p + c) + ∂p (−u) = 0, so Liouville’s formula gives unit volume. But H(u,b −p) =
 b p) − 2cp, so the Hamiltonian is not even in momentum. If (u(t), p(t)) is a solution,
H(u,
the putative reversed path (u(−t), −p(−t)) has first derivative −u̇(−t) = −(p(−t) + c),
whereas the equation evaluated on the reversed state requires −p(−t) + c. They differ by
2c. Momentum-flip reversibility fails although volume is preserved.

Proposition 51.8 (The ordinary energy ratio is incomplete for a general map). Let F
be a differentiable involution but do not assume it preserves volume. The deterministic
Metropolis acceptance that balances ρF is
                                                               
                                          ρF (F x)| det DF (x)|
                          αJ (x) = min 1,                         .             (51.28)
                                                 ρF (x)

Thus the energy-only ratio (51.7) is justified only when the absolute Jacobian determinant
is one.

Proof. The accepted mass density sent from x to y = F (x) is ρF (x)αJ (x)dx. Since
dy = | det DF (x)|dx, balance with the reverse accepted mass requires

                        ρF (x)αJ (x) = ρF (F x)αJ (F x)| det DF (x)|.                  (51.29)

Involution implies | det DF (F x)| = | det DF (x)|−1 . Substituting (51.28) on both sides
gives the same minimum of ρF (x) and ρF (F x)| det DF (x)|, proving balance. Removing
the Jacobian is valid only when it equals one.

   For a proposal that is neither an involution nor otherwise supplied with a tractable
reverse proposal density, even (51.28) is not enough. One must construct an involutive
extension, randomize over forward/reverse directions with the right law, or use the full
Hastings ratio. Therefore “evaluate the true posterior at the endpoint” is not a general
correctness theorem.

51.6      The filtering boundary
The proposal proof and the target definition are separate obligations. Even a perfect
proposal kernel is exact only for the scalar placed in its MH ratio. This section states
that boundary precisely.
   Let the latent state-space model be

                                              x0 ∼ µ u ,                                (51.38)
                                      xt | xt−1 ∼ fu (· | xt−1 ),                       (51.39)
                                         yt | xt ∼ gu (· | xt ),                        (51.40)

with exact likelihood
                                 Z               T
                                                 Y
                        L(u) =       µu (dx0 )         fu (dxt | xt−1 )gu (yt | xt ).   (51.41)
                                                 t=1

The exact unconstrained posterior is

                                     π(u | y) ∝ p(u)L(u)eJ(u) .                         (51.42)

51.6.1     Deterministic exact and approximate filters
Let a deterministic filter F return a positive scalar LF (u). Define

                                 πF (u | y) ∝ p(u)LF (u)eJ(u) .                         (51.43)

Proposition 51.11 (Exactness relative to the declared deterministic filter). If the end-
point correction in Proposition 51.4 evaluates UF (u) = − log p(u) − log LF (u) − J(u)
deterministically, the kernel leaves πF invariant. It leaves the exact posterior (51.42)
invariant by this argument only if LF (u) = cL(u) almost everywhere for a constant c > 0
independent of u.
Proof. The first claim is Proposition 51.4 with the named potential. The normalized
densities πF and π are equal if their unnormalized likelihood factors differ by a positive
u-independent constant. Conversely, if the priors and charts agree and the two normalized
posterior densities are equal wherever the prior is positive, then their likelihood ratio is
the ratio of their normalizing constants and is therefore constant almost everywhere.
   Thus a Kalman filter for the declared linear Gaussian model can supply the exact L.
A UKF, SGQF, assumed-density filter, deterministic particle flow, or fixed low-rank filter
ordinarily supplies a named LF ̸= L. Corrected neural-force HMC can be exact for that
approximate-filter posterior, not for the latent model posterior. The MH step corrects
the trajectory surrogate; it does not correct the filtering approximation.

51.6.2     Fixed randomness and relaxed filters
Suppose a randomized program returns L(u;
                                      b ω) for random numbers ω. Freezing one
realization ω0 makes

reverse laws. A neural force may propose u conditional on retained ω, but correctness
then depends on a complete extended-state kernel, not on Proposition 51.4 applied only
to u.

Proposition 51.14 (Fresh noisy endpoint values do not define the deterministic MH
ratio). Replacing LF (u) in (51.7) by independent fresh estimates at the current and pro-
posed states is not, in general, a valid implementation of either deterministic HMC for π
or pseudo-marginal MCMC for π     e.
Proof. The deterministic proof fails because the acceptance probability is random con-
ditional on (u, p) and is not a function of one fixed target density. The pseudo-marginal
proof fails because the estimator realization at the current state is part of the extended
state and must be retained on rejection; redrawing it changes the denominator without
an extended-state proposal ratio. Only special noisy-MCMC constructions with their
own balance proof avoid this conclusion for π e.
